papers.title: Residual Language Abilities Correlate With Diagnosis and Prognosis in Patients With Disorders of Consciousness.
papers.abstract: Evaluating residual consciousness and predicting outcomes in unresponsive patients pose significant clinical challenges. Language assessment is crucial for these patients, and language-based EEG paradigms have shown promise in aiding diagnosis and prognosis in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). However, current language-based EEG paradigms either require higher-order cognitive functions, thereby misidentifying some conscious patients as unconscious, or rely on automatic processing, which fails to capture residual consciousness in DoC. Newly developed, simple phrase sequences combined with neural frequency tagging were used to explore a language paradigm tailored to a critical processing threshold. This paradigm was designed to reflect the dynamic process of consciousness in DoC, while requiring minimal cognitive load. Our results showed that significant phrase-level EEG responses were observed in healthy subjects, MCS patients, and UWS patients in three conditions. Neural tracking of phrase structure showed a progressive decrease across three groups (healthy > MCS > UWS). Among the UWS patients, 52.38% (11 out of 21) and among the MCS patients, 45.83% (11 out of 24) exhibited significant ITPC at the syllable rate in at least one of the three conditions. Additionally, 38.10% (8 out of 21) of UWS patients and 33.33% (8 out of 24) of MCS patients demonstrated significant ITPC at the phrase rate. The language paradigm performance in this study was superior to that of other paradigms in detecting the proportion of residual language ability in DoC patients. Furthermore, cortical tracking at the phrase rate significantly correlated with 12-month outcomes and effectively classified patients according to their 12-month prognosis. The simplified language assessment demonstrates strong potential to detect residual language ability in DoC patients and could potentially be used to detect residual consciousness and determine prognosis in unresponsive patients.

papers.title: Self-reported acceptable pain intensity is associated with psychosocial burden beyond pain severity in chronic pain patients: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Self-reported acceptable pain intensity is collected as part of intake procedures in some pain clinic settings, yet has rarely been examined in relation to psychosocial outcomes. This study investigated whether acceptable pain intensity is associated with psychosocial symptom burden (somatization, anxiety, sleep impairment, perceived stress, depression, and pain-related disability) in chronic pain patients after adjusting for pain severity and trauma history. Secondary analysis of 822 chronic pain patients from a German university pain clinic (previously published cohort). Acceptable pain (visual analogue scale [VAS], 0-100) was examined in relation to somatization (PHQ-15), anxiety (GAD-7), sleep impairment (VAS), perceived stress (PHQ-Stress), depression (PHQ-9), and disability (Pain Disability Index) in multivariable regression models adjusted for three pain intensity measures, trauma category, age, and sex. Acceptable pain was scaled per 10-point VAS increment. Bonferroni correction was applied (α = 0.008). Post-hoc trauma × acceptable pain interactions were tested. Higher acceptable pain was associated with greater somatization (B = 0.37, 95% CI 0.19-0.55, p < .001), anxiety (B = 0.30, 0.11-0.48, p = .002), sleep impairment (B = 1.75, 0.67-2.84, p = .002), and perceived stress (B = 0.23, 0.09-0.37, p = .002), but not with depression (p = .054) or disability (p = .82). Findings were consistent across three prespecified sensitivity analyses. An exploratory post-hoc interaction test suggested that the acceptable pain-depression association was more pronounced in higher trauma categories (Bonferroni-significant trauma × acceptable pain interaction, p < .001). Higher self-reported acceptable pain intensity is associated with elevated psychosocial symptom burden beyond pain severity, with significant adjusted associations for somatization, anxiety, sleep impairment, and perceived stress, but not for depression or disability. Although the incremental contribution was small, the direction of the association was consistent across the four significant outcomes. Higher acceptable pain should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of better coping. Instead, it may reflect heterogeneous processes such as low outcome expectations, resigned tolerability, or psychosocial vulnerability, particularly among patients in higher trauma categories; shared method variance cannot be excluded. Prospective validation is needed.

papers.title: The whole day matters, but so do living conditions: reframing the 24-hour movement through an equity lens.
papers.abstract: The 24-hour movement approach has strengthened physical activity science by integrating physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep within the day's finite time. This Comment argues that its major contribution is also its main limitation. By treating the day as a composition of movement states, the approach extends the energy-expenditure definition of physical activity into a more complete, yet still behavior-centered, account of daily life. Physical activity should also be understood as a population condition shaped by governments, institutions, and markets through access to opportunity. This shift matters because individuals do not simply allocate movement, sitting, and sleep; labor, transport, housing, safety, gender, income, climate, commercial forces, and public infrastructure structure these activities. Moreover, in low-income settings and low- and middle-income countries, necessity often shapes activity, while choice-constrained conditions frequently limit leisure-time or volitional activity. A more equitable 24-hour framework should therefore move from movement behaviors alone to 24-hour living conditions, asking not only how time is spent but also how opportunity is distributed.
papers.journal: The international journal of behavioral nutrition and physical activity

papers.title: Insomnia in medical students during an examination period: associations with depression, dysfunctional sleep beliefs, and academic performance.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is common among medical students and is linked to impaired mental health and academic functioning. Medical students are exposed to persistent psychosocial stress, yet the extent to which state factors (e.g., stress, mood) versus trait factors (e.g., chronotype, sleep beliefs) contribute to insomnia severity is unclear. While dysfunctional sleep beliefs are relatively stable cognitive traits, they remain amenable to targeted interventions. We conducted a cross-sectional survey at a German medical school during a fourth year exam period. Students completed the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI; primary outcome), selected items of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-2 (GAD-2), a visual analogue scale (VAS) for stress, the Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep Scale-16 (DBAS-16), and reduced the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ); academic performance was recorded. Group differences were tested with t tests and chi-square tests. A multivariable linear regression modeled insomnia severity (ISI) as a function of state and trait variables; a secondary model examined DBAS-16 subscales. Of 124 students, 46.0% (57/124) screened positive for clinically relevant insomnia symptoms (ISI > 10). Students with clinically relevant inomnias symptoms had shorter total sleep time (391.0 ± 76.5 vs. 438.2 ± 58.3 min; P < 0.001), longer sleep onset latency (51.1 ± 37.1 vs. 21.6 ± 18.0 min; P < 0.001), and lower sleep efficiency (82.2% ± 12.2% vs. 90.1% ± 7.2%; P < 0.001). In adjusted analyses (R² = 0.572; adjusted R² = 0.523), higher PHQ-9 (β = 0.30; P = 0.01) and DBAS-16 (β = 0.28; P < 0.001) were independently associated with higher ISI, whereas higher sleep efficiency (β = -0.30; P < 0.001) and academic performance (β = -0.15; P = 0.037) were inversely associated; perceived stress, anxiety, and chronotype were not independent correlates. In the DBAS-16 subscale model (R² = 0.332; adjusted R² = 0.307), Worry/Helplessness and Perceived Consequences were significantly associated with higher ISI. Clinically relevant insomnia symptoms were frequent among medical students. Depressive symptoms and dysfunctional sleep beliefs were key correlates of insomnia severity, and academic performance was inversely related. These findings suggest that sleep health and mental well-being deserve attention in medical education and student health services.

papers.title: Sleep duration and prevalent osteoporosis among U.S. postmenopausal women: a cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 2007-2018 with assessment of potential effect modification by physical activity.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sleep duration may be associated with osteoporosis. This study aimed to evaluate the nonlinear association between sleep duration and osteoporosis prevalence in postmenopausal women and to further examine whether this association differed according to physical activity (PA) status. This cross-sectional study included 4,775 postmenopausal women from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2007-2018. Using the NHANES complex survey design and examination weights, we applied survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models to examine the association between sleep duration and osteoporosis. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to evaluate potential nonlinear associations and threshold effects. PA-stratified analyses, interaction tests, and joint association analyses were further performed. Multiple sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the findings. In the fully adjusted model, both short sleep duration (OR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.26-2.14, P < 0.001) and long sleep duration (OR = 2.90, 95% CI: 1.55-5.43, P = 0.001) were associated with higher odds of prevalent osteoporosis compared with moderate sleep duration. RCS analyses indicated a U-shaped association between sleep duration and prevalent osteoporosis (P for overall = 0.0002; P for nonlinearity = 0.0003), with the lowest estimated odds at approximately 7.16 h/night. High PA was independently associated with lower odds of prevalent osteoporosis. PA may modify the association between sleep duration and prevalent osteoporosis (P for interaction = 0.010). In PA-stratified analyses, among women with high PA, the ORs for prevalent osteoporosis were 2.02 (95% CI: 1.36-2.99) for short sleep and 6.60 (95% CI: 3.03-14.38) for long sleep, compared with moderate sleep duration. The corresponding ORs among women with low PA were 1.38 (95% CI: 0.95-2.01) and 1.68 (95% CI: 0.88-3.21), respectively. Joint analyses indicated that women with both high PA and moderate sleep duration had the lowest odds of prevalent osteoporosis. Among postmenopausal women in the United States (US), sleep duration was associated with osteoporosis prevalence in a U-shaped manner. Both short and long sleep duration were associated with higher odds of osteoporosis. PA may modify this association. Sleep duration and PA should be considered jointly in observational assessments of lifestyle factors associated with bone health. Not applicable.

papers.title: Circadian melatonin suppression and vitamin D deficiency disrupt aortic reactivity via MT1/MT2 and VDR-dependent mechanisms in rats.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and vitamin D deficiency (VDD) are increasingly prevalent and independently associated with cardiovascular dysfunction. However, their combined impact on vascular reactivity and receptor signaling remains insufficiently defined. This study investigated the independent and interactive effects of melatonin (MEL) suppression induced by continuous light (CL) or pinealectomy (Px) and VDD on vascular contractility, endothelial function, and MT1/vitamin D receptor (VDR) gene expression in rat thoracic aorta. Isolated aortic rings were subjected to cumulative concentration response curves for phenylephrine (PE) and acetylcholine (ACh). Pharmacodynamic parameters, potency (pD₂), maximal efficacy (Emax), and area under the curve (AUC) were calculated. MEL and calcitriol modulation with receptor antagonism was performed to determine receptor dependence. Relative MT1 and VDR mRNA expression was quantified using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). CL, Px, and VDD significantly enhanced PE-induced maximal contraction, with the combined deficiency groups exhibiting the greatest augmentation of α₁-adrenergic responsiveness. In contrast, ACh-induced relaxation was selectively impaired under dual-deficiency conditions, characterized by reduced Emax without major changes in pD2, indicating compromised endothelial efficacy rather than altered receptor sensitivity. MEL attenuated vasoconstriction and enhanced relaxation in a receptor-dependent manner, whereas calcitriol potentiated contractility through VDR signaling. Notably, combined CL + VDD produced marked upregulation of MT1 (~ 10-fold) and VDR (~ 108-fold), suggesting compensatory transcriptional remodeling. Circadian disruption and VDD synergistically promote vascular hyperreactivity and endothelial dysfunction. Their convergence amplifies α₁-adrenergic signaling while impairing nitric oxide (NO) mediated relaxation, identifying a mechanistic axis linking modern light exposure and hypovitaminosis D to heightened cardiovascular risk.
papers.journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology

papers.title: Lower intradaily rest-activity variability is associated with severe periodontitis: A cross-sectional wrist-accelerometry study.
papers.abstract: Behavioral research on periodontitis has largely emphasized sleep duration and activity volume, whereas the 24-hour temporal organization of movement and rest remains understudied. We examined wrist-accelerometry-derived intradaily variability (IV) in relation to severe periodontitis. This cross-sectional study included 4,631 adults aged 30 years or older from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2014. Participants had wrist-accelerometry data and an evaluable full-mouth periodontal examination. Severe periodontitis was defined using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/American Academy of Periodontology surveillance definition. Survey-weighted logistic regression with marginal standardization estimated adjusted prevalence measures. Severe periodontitis was identified in 507 participants (survey-weighted prevalence, 7.69%). In the fully adjusted model, standardized prevalence was 7.41% when IV was set to the analytic-cohort mean and 5.83% when IV was set to the mean plus 1 standard deviation. The adjusted marginal prevalence ratio was 0.786 (95% confidence interval, 0.696-0.889), and the prevalence difference was - 1.58% points (95% confidence interval, - 2.32 to - 0.85). Quartile results were broadly inverse but not strictly monotonic, and the restricted cubic spline showed no statistical evidence of nonlinearity. Higher IV was cross-sectionally associated with a lower standardized prevalence of severe periodontitis, although the absolute difference was modest. The findings do not establish temporal direction or support clinical intervention; longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether IV adds information beyond established periodontal risk indicators.
keywords: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey

papers.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for anxiety symptoms across fear, trauma, and disease contexts: a narrative review of clinical evidence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Anxiety symptoms occur in primary anxiety disorders as well as fear-, trauma-, and disease-related contexts, creating a need for safe and accessible non-pharmacological interventions. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation approach that may influence central and autonomic networks through auricular vagal pathways. This narrative review summarizes clinical evidence, stimulation parameters, safety findings, and potential mechanisms of taVNS for anxiety symptoms across these contexts. Peer-reviewed studies were identified through searches of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus up to June 2026. Eligible original human studies examining taVNS in anxiety symptoms, anxiety disorders, fear-learning paradigms, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)-related symptoms, and comorbid or disease-related anxiety were synthesized narratively. Key methodological features, stimulation protocols, comparators, safety findings, and quantitative outcomes were extracted when available. Current evidence suggests that taVNS may improve selected anxiety-related symptoms, fear-extinction processes, PTSD-related hyperarousal, sleep outcomes, and autonomic nervous system parameters. Short-term studies generally report acceptable tolerability, with mostly mild adverse events. However, stimulation protocols, control designs, and outcome measures varied across studies. taVNS may be a promising adjunctive approach for anxiety symptoms across heterogeneous clinical and experimental contexts. Larger sham-controlled studies with standardised parameters and longer follow-up are needed to clarify efficacy, optimal stimulation protocols, and long-term safety.
papers.journal: European archives of psychiatry and clinical neuroscience

papers.title: Human-artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time.
papers.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

papers.title: Association between caregiving duration and hypertension among family caregivers: the TMM CommCohort study.
papers.abstract: With the global increase in elderly individuals requiring long-term care, family caregivers face significant physical and psychosocial burdens. This study examined the association between caregiving duration and hypertension using three indices: morning and evening home blood pressure (HBP) and research blood pressure (BP). This cross-sectional study included 13,518 participants from the Tohoku Medical Megabank Community-Based Cohort Study. Caregiving time was categorized via questionnaire. Hypertension was defined according to the Japanese Society of Hypertension Guidelines for the Management of Elevated Blood Pressure and Hypertension 2025 (HBP ≥ 135/85 mmHg, research BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg, or medication use). Multivariable robust Poisson regression estimated prevalence ratios (PRs), adjusted for demographics, lifestyle and social psychological factors. Participants providing care "almost all day" had significantly higher PRs for morning (PR: 1.26; 95% CI: 1.07-1.48) and evening hypertension (PR: 1.27; 95% CI: 1.03-1.56) than non-caregivers. Notably, no significant association was observed with research BP-defined hypertension. Stratified analyses revealed that these associations were particularly prominent among caregivers aged <65 years (P-interaction for morning hypertension = 0.003). The interaction between sex and caregiving time was not significant. Prolonged caregiving burden is associated with a higher prevalence of hypertension in the morning and evening, particularly among working-age caregivers. Because these risks were not captured by research BP, HBP monitoring is essential for cardiovascular risk management in caregivers. Social policies and clinical interventions should target younger caregivers to mitigate the physiological strain of 24-h caregiving responsibilities.
papers.journal: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension

papers.title: Structural basis of the gating mechanism of the large-conductance mechanosensitive channel from Escherichia coli.
papers.abstract: The mechanosensitive channel of large conductance (MscL) is a tension-gated, pore-forming protein that acts as a safety valve to protect bacteria from osmotic lysis. Escherichia coli MscL (EcMscL) was the first mechanosensitive channel discovered and subsequently served as a model system for understanding mechanical sensing, becoming one of the most decorated and well-studied systems. Despite extensive biophysical and functional characterisation spanning several decades, the precise mechanism of EcMscL gating has been poorly understood due to the lack of high-resolution structural information. Herein, we solve two EcMscL structures by cryoEM in the closed conformation in DMPC and DOPC lipid nanodiscs. Using PELDOR/DEER spectroscopy, we screen conditions and identify that in DSPC lipids, the EcMscL conformational ensemble shifts away from the closed state and that open-like states are present. We solve the structure in an expanded state by cryoEM, revealing an architecture with pore properties consistent with previous electrophysiology reports. By combining hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the dynamics of EcMscL gating in lipid bilayers, identifying sites involved in the closed-to-expanded transition. Combined, this enables us to inform on the elusive structural mechanism of EcMscL mechanosensitive channel function.

papers.title: [Compound Danshen Cataplasm promoting acclimatization to high-altitude environments].
papers.abstract: To address acute mountain sickness(AMS) easily induced by low pressure, hypoxia, and intense ultraviolet radiation in high-altitude environments, a novel Compound Danshen Cataplasm(CDC) was developed, and its adhesive properties were evaluated. The hippocampal neuron(HT22) hypoxia model and small-animal hypoxia model were established. The anti-hypoxia and anti-AMS efficacy of CDC was assessed by an open field test, novel object recognition test, routine blood examination, sleep duration measurement, determination of brain and lung wet-to-dry ratios, detection of inflammatory and oxidative stress factors, and pathological section observation. In addition, network pharmacology and molecular docking simulations were employed to explore the underlying mechanism of action. The results show that CDC can significantly increase the survival rate of HT22 cells under hypoxia, reduce cell apoptosis, improve spontaneous exploration ability and cognitive function of hypoxic model mice, prolong sleep duration under hypoxic conditions, promote blood cell recovery, alleviate brain and lung edema, significantly reduce the levels of TNF-α, i NOS, IL-6, and MDA in blood, brain tissue, and lung tissue of mice, increase SOD activity(P<0. 01), and markedly alleviate hypoxia-induced brain and lung edema as well as inflammatory cell infiltration. Network pharmacology results reveal that the binding energies between key active components of CDC and core disease targets are all less than-5 k J·mol~(-1), and that CDC can downregulate the protein expression levels of relevant genes STAT3, JAK1, JAK2, and their phosphorylated forms in the brain tissue of mice. In conclusion, CDC can meet the need for prolonged efficacy under urgent and special conditions, demonstrating significant potential application value.
papers.journal: Zhongguo Zhong yao za zhi = Zhongguo zhongyao zazhi = China journal of Chinese materia medica

papers.title: Upper Airway Muscle Stiffness in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Assessed by Shear Wave Elastography.
papers.abstract: In obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), characterized by recurrent episodes of apnea and hypopnea, the activity of the upper airway dilator muscles is significant. In our study, we aimed to compare shear wave elastography (SWE) values of the genioglossus (GG), geniohyoid (GH), and mylohyoid (MH) muscles in patients with OSA. In this prospective study, 90 adults who underwent full-night polysomnography were included. Participants were classified as non-OSA (apnea-hypopnea index [AHI] <5, n = 32) or OSA (AHI ≥5, n = 58), and OSA patients were further divided by severity. SWE was used to assess the stiffness of the bilateral GG, bilateral MH, and GH muscles. Bilateral GG and GH stiffness values were significantly higher in OSA patients than in non-OSA individuals, whereas bilateral MH measurements did not differ between groups (P < .001, .006, and .004, respectively). Among OSA subgroups, left GG stiffness was significantly higher in severe OSA than in mild-moderate OSA (P = .043). Right GG stiffness showed positive correlations with AHI and supine AHI (r = 0.392 and r = 0.491, respectively; both P < .001). Left GG stiffness was positively correlated with AHI and rapid eye movement-AHI (r = 0.338, P = .001; r = 0.423, P < .001). GH stiffness was positively correlated with both AHI and oxygen desaturation index (r = 0.313, P = .003; r = 0.302, P = .004). SWE may provide a useful non-invasive tool for evaluating upper airway muscle characteristics in OSA. Associations between upper airway muscle stiffness and polysomnographic parameters were observed; however, these cross-sectional findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating, requiring confirmation in larger studies.
papers.journal: Journal of ultrasound in medicine : official journal of the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine

papers.title: Development and psychometric analysis of the Maternal Attitude Scale Toward Infant Massage (MASTIM).
papers.abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate the Maternal Attitude Scale Toward Infant Massage (MASTIM). This methodological and correlational study included mothers with infants aged 0-12 months in Turkey, between August 2025 and February 2026. The psychometric properties of the scale were evaluated using the Content Validity Index (CVI) for content validity, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses (EFA, CFA) for construct validity, and Cronbach's α, item-total correlations, independent samples t-tests for reliability. The scale consists of 15 items and five factors. The Cronbach's alpha coefficient for "Sleep" was 0.82, "Growth and Development" was 0.90, "Bonding" was 0.84, "Digestion and Elimination" was 0.79, "Colic" was 0.80 and the total score was 0.88.The content validity index (CVI) for MASTIM items ranged from 0.88 to 0.96. The MASTIM scale was found to be a valid and reliable instrument for assessing maternal attitudes toward infant massage. MASTIM provides a practical tool for assessing maternal attitudes toward infant massage, enabling pediatric nursing and healthcare professionals to support and monitor mother-infant interaction in clinical settings.

papers.title: Obesity, Weight Loss, and Perioperative Risk Assessment in Otolaryngology.
papers.abstract: Obesity is associated with unique and compounding perioperative challenges in otolaryngologic surgery. This review summarizes evidence-based guidance on preoperative risk stratification, airway management, intraoperative anesthetic and ventilatory strategies, and procedure-specific postoperative care for patients with obesity undergoing otolaryngologic surgery, with emphasis on the emerging phenotype of sarcopenic obesity, the shared airway, and individualized monitoring frameworks.

papers.title: Lifestyle Interventions and Otolaryngologic Care for Adults with Obesity or Overweight.
papers.abstract: Obesity is associated with numerous otolaryngologic conditions, including obstructive sleep apnea, chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media, and laryngopharyngeal reflux disease, through mechanisms involving chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, mechanical airway compromise, and metabolic dysregulation. This review examines the evidence linking obesity to otolaryngologic disorders and explores lifestyle interventions relevant to otolaryngologic care. While the strongest evidence supports weight loss for obstructive sleep apnea, benefits extend to other conditions. Practical strategies for integrating lifestyle medicine screening, counseling, and referral pathways into otolaryngology practice are discussed.

papers.title: Standardizing wearable sleep data for clinical, research, and public health use: A World Sleep Society specification.
papers.abstract: Consumer health trackers (CHTs) capable of estimating sleep have become widely adopted and are increasingly used by individuals, researchers, and healthcare professionals to characterize habitual sleep patterns and their relationship to health. Although many manufacturers report similarly named sleep measures, these are often defined, computed, and represented differently across the industry, hindering interpretation. Population reference values, risk thresholds, and outcome associations can only be established reliably when measurements are standardized to represent the same underlying constructs. To address this standardization gap, a multidisciplinary working group comprising academic and industry experts developed a minimum viable standard, specifying a common semantic framework for Fundamental Sleep Measures generated by CHTs. The proposed specification balances scientific rigor, clinical utility, and practical implementation while accommodating proprietary algorithms and user interfaces. By standardizing backend data semantics rather than frontend product implementation, the framework enables interoperability across manufacturers without constraining innovation and product differentiation. The standard specifies metadata, provenance, quality indicators, and circumstances in which wearable-derived sleep measures should be interpreted with greater caution. It provides the technical foundation for consistent integration of CHT sleep data into electronic health records, digital health platforms, and population health systems.

papers.title: Oxygen and redox regulation of plant thermomorphogenesis.
papers.abstract: Plant thermomorphogenesis represents the adjustment of growth to warm ambient temperatures. The mechanism has long been organised around the transcription factor PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) and the thermosensors that act upon it. Internal circadian control and external light intensity and quality have been the primary contexts that gate thermosensor-PIF signal transduction. Here, we argue that cellular oxygen and the reduction/oxidation (redox) state of the cell form additional layers that gate or calibrate thermosensing signal transduction. Current evidence points to discrete mechanisms across spatial or developmental contexts, through which oxygen availability or redox-dependent protein modifications control thermomorphogenic signalling, largely downstream of or independent of PIF4. Logical argument suggests that significant mechanisms and crosstalk between oxygen and redox signalling and thermosensing remain to be revealed.

papers.title: Effects of acetazolamide on respiratory events and sleep in highlanders with obstructive sleep apnoea: a randomised controlled trial.
Effect of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation on perioperative psychological symptoms in patients undergoing elective thoracoscopic lung resection: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Perioperative anxiety is highly prevalent in patients undergoing thoracoscopic lung resection, adversely affecting postoperative recovery. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulatory intervention with demonstrated efficacy in various psychiatric and stress-related conditions. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of taVNS in reducing perioperative anxiety in this population. This single-center, parallel-group, randomized, double-blind, superiority trial was conducted at the Department of Anesthesiology and Thoracic Surgery, the Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University between October 10, 2024, and April 30, 2025. A total of 176 eligible patients aged ≥18 years with ASA physical status I-III and scheduled for elective thoracoscopic lung resection were enrolled. Patients with neuropsychiatric disorders, auricular lesions, severe cardio-cerebrovascular diseases, implanted electronic devices, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score <15, long-term psychotropic medication use or postural tachycardia syndrome were excluded. All participants were randomly allocated to receive four sessions of either active taVNS or sham taVNS. Stimulation was delivered via the auricular branch of the vagus nerve at the cymba conchae of the left ear at four predefined perioperative time points: the afternoon before surgery, the morning of surgery, immediately after tracheal extubation, and the afternoon of the first postoperative day. The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative anxiety, assessed from the initiation of the first taVNS session through 3 days postoperatively. All participants, healthcare providers, outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded to group assignment during the whole study. A total of 176 patients were randomly assigned, with 88 participants in the active taVNS group and 88 in the sham taVNS group. After excluding 2 patients (1 patient from each group) who were transferred to the ICU postoperatively, a total of 174 patients (median age, 58 years; 105 women [60.4%]) completed the study and were analysed for the primary outcome, including 87 patients in each group. The incidence of perioperative anxiety was significantly lower in the active taVNS group than in the sham taVNS group (50.6% vs. 73.6%; relative risk [RR], 0.59; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41-0.85; χ2 = 9.76; P = 0.002). Compared with sham stimulation, active taVNS was associated with reductions in anxiety and depression scores, postoperative pain intensity, and physiological stress indices and improvement in sleep quality and overall postoperative recovery. No severe adverse events were observed in either group. The main mild adverse reactions included nausea, vomiting, local tingling, dizziness and headache, and the incidence of adverse events was similar between the two groups. Four perioperative sessions of taVNS applied to the left cymba conchae significantly reduced the incidence of perioperative anxiety in patients undergoing thoracoscopic lung resection and were additionally associated with improvements in depressive symptoms, stress burden, sleep quality, and pain outcomes. Chinese Clinical Trial Register Identifier: ChiCTR2400090542 (http://www.chictr.org.cn).

papers.title: Lighting and circadian cues shape locomotor strategies for balance and navigation in larval zebrafish.
papers.abstract: Most fish are inherently unstable and must swim to stabilize posture. How diurnal fish reduce activity at night while maintaining postural control remains unclear. We defined distinct locomotor strategies that larval zebrafish (Danio rerio) use to control posture and navigate the water column in response to light and circadian cues. In the dark, larvae maintain balance by swimming in long bouts with large nose-up rotations, compensating for nose-down drift accrued during prolonged inactivity. Effective postural compensation requires vestibular sensation from the utricle. By contrast, in the light, larvae navigate with short, frequent and variable bouts. While lighting exerts a dominant, masking effect on the locomotor strategies, circadian rhythms modulate swim kinematics. Our results reveal distinct light-dark locomotor strategies and disentangle how ambient light and the internal clock jointly shape balance control and navigation. This work lays the foundation for understanding how external and internal cues interact to govern locomotor activity in freely moving diurnal animals.

papers.title: An Adolescent With Neurosyphilis.
papers.abstract: Neurosyphilis is a central nervous system (CNS) infection that has become exceedingly rare in the postantibiotic era, especially in children and HIV-negative persons. It can develop during any stage of an untreated syphilis infection and is known as "the great imitator" for its highly variable clinical presentation with inconsistent lab and imaging findings. We describe the case of a previously healthy 17-year-old boy who presented with 2 weeks of right thumb and middle finger myoclonus followed by right upper extremity focal seizures with secondary generalization. Routine and confidential psychosocial history using the HEADSS (Home; Education, Eating, and Exercise; Activities; Drugs; Sexuality; Suicide and Sleep) assessment revealed that our patient was sexually active with one female partner, prompting sexually transmitted infection (STI) screening. The final diagnosis of neurosyphilis was made following a reactive rapid plasma reagin screen and confirmatory treponemal testing of the cerebrospinal fluid. In light of the recent rise in syphilis case incidence and the devastating consequences of CNS involvement, neurosyphilis should be considered in the differential diagnoses for all sexually active adolescents with unexplained neurologic symptoms. Additionally, this case highlights the importance of comprehensive and confidential social history taking in all adolescents, as well as regular STI screening for those at risk.

papers.title: Relief Emerges as an Offset-Locked Emotional Response: Self-Reported and Neural Evidence.
papers.abstract: Relief is commonly characterized as a sustained, low-arousal positive state; yet this static view obscures the dynamic temporal structure that emerges at stimulus termination. This study investigated the self-reported and neural dynamics of relief in 30 healthy adults using an offset-locked paradigm. Continuous self-reports and high-temporal-resolution electroencephalography (EEG) were recorded during the comparison of abrupt stimulus offsets with transient intensity modulations and sustained stimulation of aversive auditory stimuli. Stimulus offsets elicited the steepest self-reported rate of change and uniquely sustained shifts in affective state. At the neural level, the change in stimulation evoked a clear N1-P2 complex, with P2 mean amplitude (200-280 ms) larger than in the sustained condition at central and medial frontal sites. This early response did not distinguish transient modulation from complete termination and is therefore best characterized as a response to acoustic change rather than to relief itself; alpha-band amplitude over longer post-change windows showed no reliable condition differences. Together, these findings provide psychophysiological evidence that relief is better characterized as a discrete, offset-locked emotional event than as a passive return to affective baseline, and suggest that the detection of stimulus change may be dissociable from the affective evaluation that follows it. These findings offer new directions for affect dynamics research and challenge static conceptualizations of relief within dimensional models of emotion.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic Reductions in Glymphatic-Related Perivascular Diffusion Across Psychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system, a perivascular pathway supporting cerebrospinal and interstitial fluid exchange and clearance, has been implicated in neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. Diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) provides a non-invasive proxy for glymphatic-related processes, yet its role in psychiatric conditions remains uncertain. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, PsycNET, and Embase for articles published up to September 25th, 2025. The protocol was pre-registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251155430). Studies reporting diffusion-based indices of glymphatic function in psychiatric populations were included. Standardised mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated for patient-control comparisons and pooled using random-effects models. Heterogeneity, methodological moderators, and risk of bias were assessed. Thirty-two studies met inclusion criteria for the systematic review, covering major psychiatric groups including mood disorders, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, psychosis, sleep disorders, and substance-related conditions. Twenty-four studies (n = 2,855; 1,503 patients, 1,352 controls) reporting bilateral DTI-ALPS measures were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled random-effects model revealed a significant transdiagnostic reduction in DTI-ALPS index in psychiatric populations compared with healthy controls (Hedges' g = -0.78, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.55, p < 0.0001). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 86.3%), and there was evidence of small-study effects. Bilateral DTI-ALPS index showed a robust but heterogeneous reduction across psychiatric disorders. These results suggest that impairments of perivascular diffusion, as indexed by DTI-ALPS, may reflect a shared transdiagnostic pattern across psychiatric conditions. Harmonised imaging pipelines and multimodal validation are needed to clarify the biological and clinical significance of these findings.

papers.title: Cortical dynamics associated with adaptive increases in clearance after obstacle contact.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate motor adaptation following obstacle contact and the underlying neural control mechanisms. 25 healthy young adults were recruited to perform an obstacle-crossing walking task, and 17 participants were included in the analysis. The gait cycle was divided into three phases: approach (the step immediately before obstacle crossing), lead (when the lead limb crosses the obstacle), and trail (when the trail limb crosses the obstacle). Power in the theta, alpha, and beta bands was calculated at electrode sites Fz, Cz, and Pz for each phase, while vertical clearance of the lead and trail limbs and horizontal distance from the obstacle were assessed as kinematic measures. Electroencephalography (EEG) and kinematic variables were compared between the 30 trials before and after obstacle contact (pre- and post-conditions). Vertical clearance of both lead and trail limbs increased significantly after obstacle contact (post-condition). In addition, theta power at Fz significantly increased during the approach phase, and the magnitude of this increase was significantly correlated with the increase in trail clearance. Beta power at Cz significantly decreased during the lead phase, but the magnitude of this change was not significantly correlated with changes in clearance. In contrast, no significant changes in EEG power were observed during the trail phase. These findings suggest that increased involvement of the frontal and motor cortices contributes to the adaptive changes following obstacle contact. Furthermore, although clearance increased in both lead and trail limbs, the underlying neural control mechanisms may differ.

papers.title: Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone Increases Dorsal Premammillary Nucleus Neuron Activity and Darting Behavior.
papers.abstract: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is classically recognized for its role in regulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis; however, it also functions as a central neuromodulator influencing arousal, locomotion, and autonomic processes. Despite these established roles, the circuit-level mechanisms through which TRH modulates behavior remain poorly defined. The dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) is a hypothalamic structure implicated in high-imminence defensive states, yet whether TRH directly engages PMd circuits is unknown. Here, we assessed the role of TRH as a modulator of PMd neuronal activity and behavioral output using in situ hybridization, electrophysiology, calcium imaging, and behavioral assays in male and female mice. TRHR mRNA was co-localized with a subset of PMd CCK-positive neurons. TRH increased firing rate in a subset of PMd neurons in brain slices, revealing functional activation of a subset of the population. This finding was corroborated by calcium imaging that showed increased activity following TRH exposure. In vivo, intrahypothalamic administration of TRH produced darting and behavioral effects. Together, these findings identify a subpopulation of PMd neurons that serve as a functional hypothalamic target of TRH signaling associated with rapid locomotor behavioral output.

papers.title: Mechanisms overcoming the resistance of human TRPV2 to chemical activation.
papers.abstract: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) is a thermosensitive cation channel widely expressed across diverse cell types. There, it contributes to numerous physiological processes and plays a role in the pathophysiology of inflammation, immunity, various cancers and neuronal development. The inherent resistance of human TRPV2 (hTRPV2) to stimuli that readily activate its rodent orthologs currently limits progress in translational and clinical research on this channel. Here, we present engineered variants of hTRPV2 that were designed to enhance channel activation induced by 2-aminoethoxydiphenylborate (2-APB), cannabidiol, and the TRPV2 agonist AV2-1, thereby identifying sites that allow for the most effective channel regulation. Through a series of rational mutations and chimeric constructs, combined with electrophysiology and molecular modeling, we identified two key allosteric sites in hTRPV2 that determine the resistance of the channel to activating stimuli. We discovered that two intracellular membrane-proximal salt bridges prevent effective activation of hTRPV2: (i) one formed between residues of the putative 2-APB-binding site and the bottom of S6 helix (R533-E647), and (ii) another formed between residues from the TRP helix and the proximal N-terminus (D655-R369). We also propose possible mechanisms by which the non-conserved pore turret contributes to channel activation. Our results may facilitate the rational drug design towards potent and selective hTRPV2 ligands and help to elucidate the functions of this channel in organs or cell types of interest.

papers.title: Effects of intensive sensorimotor rehabilitation in resting state functional connectivity in a rodent model of Cerebral Palsy.
papers.abstract: Background Sensorimotor stimulation has been shown to protect against brain damage and function impairments following experimental Cerebral Palsy (CP). Functional ultrasound (fUS) gives valuable information about brain connectivity at unprecedented spatial and time resolutions with high translational potential. We tested brain function and connectivity using fUS following experimental CP and the effects of early sensorimotor rehabilitation in the model. Methods Pregnant Wistar rats were exposed to maternal immune challenge at E18-19. Pups received perinatal anoxia at postnatal day 0 (P0) and restriction of the hindlimbs from P2 to P21. Rehabilitation (EETT) used environmental enrichment (EE) and Treadmill Training (TT) from P21 to P28. At P29, fUS was performed to access brain connectivity and graph theoretic analysis was used to distinguish patterns of brain connectivity. Results CP increased intrinsic brain functional connectivity compared to Controls and EETT animals. Connectivity was increased in CP animals in cortical areas related to sensorimotor function and subcortical myelinated structures. EETT animals showed levels of brain connectivity similar to Controls. Conclusions Sensorimotor stimulation changed brain hyperconnectivity profile induced by CP. Brain connectivity pattern alterations can be detected using fUS with high accuracy, suggesting great potential to be used as earlier biomarker for neurodevelopmentalal disorders such as CP.

papers.title: Default mode network mechanisms of trait rumination in treatment-resistant depression and rTMS: evidence from source-localized EEG.
papers.abstract: Rumination is a transdiagnostic feature of multiple psychiatric disorders and is a critical risk factor for more severe episodes and poor treatment outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) ameliorates both depressive and ruminative symptoms in TRD. While prior literature has linked rumination to abnormal default mode network (DMN) connectivity, the electrophysiological correlates of rumination in the DMN are not well understood. Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) data were examined in a cohort of 66 TRD subjects who underwent 30 sessions of rTMS treatment for TRD administered to left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We employed source-localization and calculated four metrics of functional connectivity (Amplitude Envelope Correlation [AEC], weighted Phase Lag Index [wPLI], magnitude-squared coherence, and Spectral Correlation Coefficient [SCC]) across five frequency bands within the DMN to identify the neural correlates of rumination in TRD. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using the Network Based Statistic (NBS). Baseline severity of rumination and depression were positively correlated, but AEC alpha band connectivity was positively associated only with baseline rumination severity and not depression. Rumination severity prior to treatment was not associated with any other connectivity metric. Severity of rumination and depression decreased following rTMS treatment, but alpha AEC connectivity did not charge after 30 sessions of rTMS treatment. Higher DMN connectivity, as measured by alpha-band AEC, is a stable trait-like neurophysiological marker of rumination that is not significantly affected by rTMS administered to left DLPFC.

papers.title: Antidepressants and Cognitive Function in Major Depressive Disorder: Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and Implications for Precision Treatment.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a core feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) and significantly impairs functional recovery. This review summarizes current evidence on the effects of antidepressants on cognitive function and discusses the underlying mechanisms. Antidepressants may exert their effects through multiple mechanisms, including modulation of monoaminergic neurotransmission, enhancement of neuroplasticity, and regulation of stress and inflammatory pathways. Available studies indicate that antidepressants differ in their cognitive benefits, with vortioxetine showing the most consistent procognitive evidence. Duloxetine, bupropion, and some augmentation strategies may also improve specific cognitive domains, though the evidence is limited. Importantly, cognitive improvement may result from direct drug effects on cognition or indirectly via alleviation of depressive symptoms, highlighting the need for mediation analyses in future research. In patients with late-life depression, vortioxetine and duloxetine have shown relatively clear benefits, and augmentation with cognitive enhancers has demonstrated some potential. The long-term cognitive protective effects of antidepressants remain unconfirmed. Immuno-metabolic depression subtypes, high-dose-related adverse effects, and comorbidity with anxiety and sleep disorders may constitute important sources of residual cognitive deficits. Emerging treatments such as ketamine, psychedelic compounds, and interventions targeting the gut-brain axis may offer new opportunities for addressing cognitive dysfunction in MDD. Current evidence is limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous cognitive assessments. Future research should prioritize large, randomized controlled trials with cognition as the primary endpoint, using standardized assessment tools. A better understanding of the cognitive profiles and mechanisms of antidepressants may support precision medicine strategies and promote functional recovery in patients with MDD.

papers.title: Chrononutrition in the aging era: Circadian regulation of metabolism, resilience, and healthy longevity.
papers.abstract: The increasing prevalence of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and age-related disorders has been linked to a growing mismatch between modern lifestyles and the biological rhythms that regulate human physiology. Chrononutrition, which explores the interaction between meal timing, circadian rhythms, and metabolism, has emerged as a promising strategy to improve metabolic health and support healthy aging. This review examines the molecular and physiological foundations of chrononutrition, focusing on the interplay between central and peripheral circadian clocks, metabolic regulation, and aging processes. We discuss the role of environmental and behavioural zeitgebers, including light exposure, feeding schedules, sleep, and physical activity, in maintaining circadian alignment and metabolic homeostasis. Attention is given to Time-Restricted Eating (TRE) and related meal-timing interventions. Current evidence indicates that aligning food intake with endogenous circadian rhythms improves insulin sensitivity, metabolic flexibility, lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation, and inflammatory balance, often independently of weight loss. Mechanistically, chrononutrition may also modulate key biological processes associated with aging, including mitochondrial function, autophagy, nutrient sensing, oxidative stress, and inflammaging. By restoring temporal organization across physiological systems, chrononutrition may enhance metabolic resilience and contribute to healthspan extension. Future studies should clarify its long-term effects on biological aging, resilience, and healthy longevity, while defining personalized interventions based on circadian phenotypes.

papers.title: Pharmacological Inhibition of Histamine N-Methyltransferase Markedly Improves Hypersomnia in a Mouse Model of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. In addition to motor symptoms, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) occurs frequently in patients with PD and severely impairs their quality of life. Current pharmacotherapies for EDS in PD are often associated with adverse effects. However, clinical studies have yielded inconsistent results, underscoring the need for safer, more effective treatment strategies. Histamine plays a pivotal role in maintaining wakefulness in the brain and is primarily inactivated by histamine N-methyltransferase (HNMT), the major enzyme responsible for histamine clearance in the central nervous system. We previously demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of HNMT markedly elevates brain histamine levels and potently promotes wakefulness in mouse models of narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia, suggesting that targeting HNMT may also be beneficial for treating hypersomnia in PD. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of HNMT ameliorates hypersomnia in a 6-hydroxydopamine-induced mouse model of PD. We first confirmed dopaminergic neuronal loss and hypersomnia during the active phase in a mouse model of PD. Pharmacological inhibition of HNMT with metoprine robustly increased wakefulness, markedly reduced NREM and REM sleep, and prolonged sleep latency. Metoprine also reduced sleep-wake bout fragmentation, indicating the sustained consolidation of wakefulness. In direct comparison, metoprine produced stronger and more sustained wake-promoting effects than other wake-promoting agents. These findings indicate that HNMT inhibition represents a promising and mechanistically distinct therapeutic approach for EDS in PD.

papers.title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight.
papers.abstract: Elucidating the neural computations underlying natural, complex movement remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Bat flight presents a formidable motor control challenge, requiring hand-like wings whose many degrees of freedom must be precisely coordinated to enable rapid three-dimensional (3D) maneuvers. Here, we performed large-scale wireless recordings from the wing motor cortex of freely flying bats, combined with 3D tracking of wing kinematics. Despite the complexity of flight control, bats repeatedly executed accurate flights through precise adjustments of individual wingbeats. Surprisingly, motor cortical activity was not dominated by the wingbeat cycle. Instead, neurons were sparsely active, exhibiting mixed selectivity for flight kinematics and variable entrainment to the wingbeat phase reaching millisecond-scale precision. This yielded a high-dimensional population code driven by successive wingbeats occupying distinct neural states. These findings reveal a mode of motor cortical population dynamics expressed during natural dexterous movement that is not well captured by prevailing views derived from constrained paradigms.

papers.title: A Personalized Recovery Intervention to Support Sleep Health in Emergency Healthcare Professionals.
papers.abstract: Optimizing sleep health in healthcare professionals is a challenge, as misalignment between endogenous circadian rhythms and exogenous work schedules undermines recovery, well-being, and performance. This study evaluated a tailored recovery intervention based on cognitive-behavioural approaches for insomnia designed to support recovery to rotating night shifts. In a randomized controlled trial (REST), 72 emergency healthcare professionals were randomized to intervention or control. The intervention combined personalized sleep-wake feedback with stress management techniques. Sleep-wake rhythms were monitored via actigraphy for 3 weeks before and 1 week after the intervention. Outcomes included objective sleep duration, self-reported sleepiness, insomnia severity, and subjective sleep quality, measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Insomnia Severity Index, and Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire. Fifty-nine participants (28 intervention, 31 control) were included in the primary analyses. Even on free nights, average nocturnal sleep duration was 6 h and 21 min, below recommended levels for adults. Compared with controls, intervention participants increased nocturnal time in bed by 37 min, 95% CI [13, 62], p = 0.003, and total sleep time by 23 min, 95% CI [4, 42], p = 0.019. Perceived sleep quality also improved for the intervention group t(55) = -7.91, p < 0.001, d = 2.06, 95% CI [1.42, 2.70], and insomnia symptoms decreased (β = -2.23, 95% CI [-4.26, -0.21], p = 0.031). These findings suggest that structured occupational recovery programs can enhance sleep health and facilitate recovery across rotating night work schedules. Integrating such interventions into training may reduce burnout, improve safety, and support workforce sustainability.

papers.title: Clinical validation of autoSCORE: A human-in-the-loop AI tool for interpretation of long-term EEG recordings.
papers.abstract: To validate autoSCORE, a convolutional neural network (SCORE-AI) implemented into a commercially available EEG reader, for analysis of long-term EEG (LT-EEG) recordings, and to evaluate it within the human-in-the-loop approach. autoSCORE automatically divides LT-EEG into 2-hour segments, labeling each as normal or as containing one or more of four abnormality categories: focal epileptiform, generalized epileptiform, focal non-epileptiform, or diffuse non-epileptiform. In abnormal segments, it also inserts markers defined by start/stop times and tagged by abnormality type. Within each category, markers can be ranked by decreasing probability. Eighty 2-hour LT-EEG segments (40 in-hospital, 40 ambulatory) from patients aged 0.9-82.3 years were analyzed by autoSCORE. The diagnostic reference standard was derived from independent conventional visual assessment by three human experts. Accuracy computed across expert-expert and AI-expert pairings, evaluated at the level of the 2-hour segments, were comparable, except for detection of focal non-epilepiform abnormality, where AI outperformed experts for identification accuracy (p = 0.019). The positive predictive value of the automated abnormality markers was 0.446-0.823. In the human-in-the-loop workflow, inspecting 10 automated markers with the highest probability in each category enabled correct identification of all abnormal segments, corresponding to 1.5%-5.5% of the full 2-hour segment. autoSCORE accurately screens LT-EEG recordings and may serve as an adjunct to human EEG interpretation to reduce the workload of human experts. autoSCORE is a validated tool that can increase the productivity and efficacy of human experts in assessment of LT-EEG to improve patient diagnosis and management strategies.
papers.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology

papers.title: Identifying potential risk factors for migraine-related vertigo in children.
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate established migraine-associated factors in children with idiopathic episodic vertigo. A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 30 children diagnosed with idiopathic episodic vertigo. Several migraine-associated clinical manifestations were evaluated. In addition, the presence of headache, the age of onset for both headache and vertigo, and the criteria for vestibular migraine were also considered. Data were compared to those of a control group, which did not exhibit vertigo. A family history of migraine, episodic syndromes, sleep disorders and motion sickness disorder were significantly more frequent in children with episodic vertigo (p = 0.001). Headache occurred in 7 patients (23.3%). The mean age at onset of the first vertigo episode was 8.57 ± 2.11, which was significantly lower (p < 0.0001) than the average age of onset for headache, recorded at 12.71 ± 1.50. Migraine headache was not reported before the age of 10 and never preceded the onset of vertigo. Only three patients (10%) met the diagnostic criteria for vestibular migraine, all of whom were older than 14 years. A thorough assessment of the migraine-associated factors investigated in this study may improve the evaluation of children with episodic vertigo. The readily accessible data, whether obtained directly or with parental assistance, support the hypothesis of a migraine-related origin of the symptoms. This investigation is essential, particularly during the pre-pubertal age, when headaches are frequently absent, thereby limiting the ability to fulfil the diagnostic criteria for vestibular migraine.

papers.title: Efficacy and adherence of mobile health-based myofunctional therapy for obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: To assess the impact of WeChat applet-based myofunctional therapy (MFT) on the efficacy and adherence of patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) compared to conventional hospital-guided programs. A parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted, enrolling 78 patients with OSA who declined continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or surgical treatment (mean age 39.44 ± 9.82 years). Participants were randomly allocated to either the mini-program intervention group (n = 39) or the non-intervention group (n = 39). Both groups underwent a 12-week oropharyngeal muscle training program that targeted the soft palate, tongue, lips, and buccal muscles. The intervention group received video-based guidance, real-time feedback, and automated compliance monitoring via a customized WeChat application, whereas the non-intervention group maintained their records using paper diaries. Outcomes, including polysomnography results, sleep scale scores, and compliance rates, were subsequently compared between the two groups. Sixty-six patients completed the study (32 in the intervention group and 34 in non-intervention group). Improvement in AHI was significantly better in the intervention group than in the non-intervention group (Δ8.92 ± 9.27 vs. Δ2.66 ± 6.80 beats/h, P < 0.001), and adherence rates were higher at all time points (12 weeks: 73% vs. 66%, P = 0.002). Mobile health guided MFT significantly improved treatment adherence in patients with OSA and outperformed traditional modality in terms of improvement in the core metric AHI, providing a digital solution for CPAP-intolerant patients.

papers.title: Siddha Varmathadaval therapy in the management of stress-related insomnia: A case report.
papers.abstract: Insomnia affects 10-30% of adults globally, with limited non-pharmacological options. This single-case report documents Siddha Varmathadaval therapy for stress-related insomnia. A 55-year-old woman presented with four-month history of insomnia (difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep) and daytime fatigue. Thookaminmai (insomnia) of Vatha-Pitham origin per Siddha principles was diagnosed. Baseline assessments showed severe insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index [ISI] = 21/28, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI] = 15/21, Athens Insomnia Scale [AIS] = 13/24, Perceived Stress Scale-10 [PSS-10] = 31/40). The patient underwent twenty-one consecutive daily Varmathadaval therapy sessions using Sukku Thailam (90-120 minutes each), administered by a trained Siddha physician. Post-therapy improvements included ISI = 8/28 (62% reduction), PSQI = 6/21 (60% reduction), AIS = 4/24 (69% reduction), and PSS-10 = 12/40 (61% reduction). Traditional Siddha parameters (Manikadai Nool, Neikuri) demonstrated progressive improvement correlating with clinical outcome. Sleep latency decreased (45 → 15 minutes) and total sleep time increased (4-5→6-7 hours). Benefits were sustained at 4-week (ISI = 9) and 12-week (ISI = 11) post-treatment follow-up, with mild stress-related variation. Varmathadaval therapy produced clinically significant, sustained improvements in stress-related insomnia. The therapy was safe and well-tolerated. Controlled trials with prospective stress assessment are warranted.
papers.journal: Journal of Ayurveda and integrative medicine

papers.title: Loss of hepatic circadian organization in fatty liver syndrome identifies CLOCK as a regulator of lipid homeostasis in laying hens.
papers.abstract: Fatty liver syndrome (FLS) is a major metabolic disorder in laying hens, but how hepatic lipid dysregulation is linked to circadian disruption remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of circadian regulation in FLS pathogenesis and focused on the core clock gene Clock Circadian Regulator (CLOCK). In a high-fat diet-induced FLS model in Lohmann pink layers, affected birds showed hepatomegaly, hepatic lipid accumulation, elevated serum total cholesterol, triglycerides, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase, increased hepatic pro-inflammatory gene expression, and reduced interleukin-10 (IL-10) expression. FLS was also accompanied by reduced laying performance, delayed and dispersed oviposition, and altered temporal profiles of reproductive hormones. Time-series liver transcriptomics across six circadian time points showed extensive transcriptional remodeling in FLS, with dysregulated genes enriched mainly in lipid metabolic and circadian pathways. Pathway analyses indicated increased fatty acid biosynthesis together with reduced fatty acid degradation, glycerophospholipid metabolism, and ether lipid metabolism. Rhythmicity analysis further revealed a marked collapse of hepatic circadian organization: the number of rhythmically expressed genes decreased from 1,046 in controls to 81 in FLS, and core clock genes including CLOCK, cryptochrome 2 (CRY2), and basic helix-loop-helix family member e40 (BHLHE40) lost rhythmic expression. Series Test of Cluster analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and protein-protein interaction analysis consistently placed CLOCK at the center of the circadian regulatory network associated with hepatic metabolic disturbance. Functional assays in primary chicken hepatocytes showed that CLOCK overexpression reduced lipid accumulation, intracellular total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and expression of lipogenic genes, while increasing peroxisome proliferation-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) expression and altering multiple circadian regulators. In an oleic acid-induced steatosis model, CLOCK overexpression similarly reduced lipid deposition and inflammatory gene expression, while increasing IL-10, nicotinamide phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT), and Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) expression. This study provides mechanistic insight into the circadian basis of FLS and highlights CLOCK as a potential molecular target for the prevention and intervention of metabolic liver disorders in poultry.

papers.title: Reported nasal obstruction is associated with multiple sleep-related symptoms but shows only a modest association with the apnea-hypopnea index.
papers.abstract: Nasal obstruction is frequently reported in patients evaluated for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but its contribution to disease severity and patient-reported symptoms remains incompletely understood. To examine the associations between reported nasal obstruction categories, assessed using the Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) score, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), sleep parameters and patient-reported symptoms. In this retrospective observational analysis of a prospective cohort, 4369 adults referred for sleep assessment with available baseline AHI data were included. Nasal obstruction was categorized as no reported obstruction, mild, moderate, or severe/extreme based on an initial screening question followed, when positive, by the Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) questionnaire. Associations between nasal obstruction categories, AHI, objective sleep parameters and patient-reported symptoms were assessed using multivariable regression models. At baseline, 3602 patients (82.4%) had no reported nasal obstruction, whereas 767 patients (17.6%) reported nasal obstruction. Among patients with nasal obstruction, 210 (27.4%) had mild obstruction, 345 (45.0%) had moderate obstruction, and 212 (27.6%) had severe obstruction. Moderate and severe nasal obstruction categories were associated with higher adjusted AHI estimates compared with no reported nasal obstruction, although these associations were modest. In contrast, nasal obstruction categories were more consistently associated with patient-reported symptoms. Moderate and severe obstruction were associated with higher sleepiness, insomnia severity, asthenia, depressive symptoms, morning headaches, dyspnea, and memory complaints. Reported nasal obstruction was associated with multiple patient-reported symptoms and, to a lesser extent, with higher adjusted AHI estimates among patients with moderate and severe nasal obstruction. These findings suggest that nasal obstruction should not be considered solely as a marker of objective OSA severity, but rather as a complementary clinical dimension capturing patient-perceived sleep-related impairment that is not fully reflected by AHI.

papers.title: Frequent chronic pain in relation to sleep disturbances: A nationally representative study of adults in the United States.
papers.abstract: Frequent chronic pain (FCP) is associated with sleep. Primarily, pain can increase stress and inflammation, impairing sleep. In turn, but less commonly, poor sleep can increase pain sensitivity, suggesting potential bidirectionality. However, the FCP-sleep relationship has not been investigated across various sociodemographic groups, especially in nationally representative samples. Using the 2013-2018 US National Health Interview Survey, we investigated FCP-sleep associations among adults. Participants self-reported musculoskeletal pain over the past three months (FCP: yes ['everyday'/'most days'] vs. no ['some days'/'never']), short sleep duration (<7-h), insomnia symptoms (difficulty falling/staying asleep ≥3 times/week), and nonrestorative sleep (NRS: waking feeling rested ≤3 days/week). Adjusting for confounders, we used survey-weighted Poisson regression with robust variance to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for associations, overall and by age, sex, and race along with ethnicity. Among 90,810 adults, mean age±SE was 48 ± 0.11 years, 24% reported FCP (64% of adults aged ≥50 years, 56% of women). FCP was associated with a higher prevalence of short sleep, with stronger associations among younger (PR18-30 years = 1.57[1.44-1.70]) vs. older adults (PR ≥ 50 years = 1.34[1.29-1.39]). FCP was associated with a higher prevalence of insomnia symptoms, especially among men (PRmen = 1.82[1.75-1.89] vs. PRwomen = 1.57[1.52-1.61]) and Hispanic/Latine (PR = 1.84[1.70-1.99]) and Black (PR = 1.79[1.66-1.92]) vs. White adults (PR = 1.63[1.58-1.67]). FCP was associated with a higher prevalence of NRS (PR = 1.66[1.62-1.69]), with stronger associations among older adults (PR ≥ 50 years = 1.73[1.67-1.79] vs. PR18-30 years = 1.61[1.52-1.70] and PR31-49years = 1.48[1.43-1.53]) and men (PRmen = 1.75[1.69-1.82] vs. PRwomen = 1.59[1.55-1.63]). There were complex associations between FCP and sleep health among US adults that varied by sociodemographic characteristics. Targeted intervention studies are warranted.

papers.title: From neural clocks to learning clocks: Educational zeitgebers in bipolar disorder.
Alcohol dependence before burn injuries: A driver of long-term psychiatric morbidity and mortality.
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder is prevalent among burn patients, with studies estimating that 30-50% present with intoxication or a history of dependence at the time of injury. However, there is a paucity of literature detailing alcohol dependence and mental health after burn injury. This study evaluated the association of alcohol dependence among burn patients with onset of psychiatric disorders as well as mortality. A retrospective analysis was conducted of a multi-institutional database of burn patients between April 2010 and June 2025. Two burn cohorts were identified: pre-existing alcohol-dependent patients and those without alcohol dependence. Individuals with pre-existing psychiatric disorders were excluded. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity-score matched for demographics, comorbidities, concurrent substance use, total body surface area burned, and procedural interventions. Risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for development of psychiatric disorders, readmission, and mortality at 3 months and 12 months post-burn, with significance set at p < 0.05. Following matching, each cohort had 6928 burn patients. At 3 months post-burn, alcohol-dependent patients had significantly higher rates of readmission (RR 1.87) as well as onset of opioid-use disorder (RR 1.91), depression (RR 2.68), anxiety (RR 2.13), PTSD (RR 2.35), adjustment disorder (RR 1.77), suicidal ideation (RR 2.82), and sleep disorders (RR 1.56) (all p < 0.05). At 12 months post-burn, all outcomes remained significant, with the addition of increased mortality (RR 1.27; p < 0.001). Alcohol dependence was associated with significant risk of developing new-onset psychiatric morbidities among burn patients without preceding psychiatric diagnosis.

papers.title: White noise as a non-pharmacological intervention for enhancing the recovery of rats with wound-associated sleep disorders.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are one of the common symptoms in patients with wounds, which can hinder recovery. Commonly used hypnotic medications in clinical practice are short-acting but carry risks of adverse reactions and drug abuse. As a non-invasive acoustic intervention, white noise can regulate brain electroencephalographic rhythms to improve sleep disorders. However, the interventional effects and rehabilitation outcomes of white noise on wounds with sleep disorders remain unclear. A wound model with sleep disorders was established in rats by integrating para-chlorophenylalanine-induced sleep deprivation with full-thickness skin excision. The rats were randomly allocated into three groups: white noise (WN), alprazolam (ALP), and control (Model). Sleep status was evaluated using pentobarbital supra-threshold dose synergistic sleep tests, circadian activity monitoring, and serum 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) level measurements. Inflammatory responses were assessed via blood routine examinations and serological analyses. Histological and immunohistochemical evaluations were performed to examine the structural features of the wounds. Compared with the control group, the WN group showed significantly reduced sleep latency and inflammatory markers, as well as increased sleep duration, body weight gain rate, and wound healing rate. After prolonged intervention, the newly formed tissue in the WN group exhibited a lower epidermal-dermal ratio, collagen fibers that were orderly and loosely arranged, decreased neovascularization, and thus more closely resembled the morphology of normal skin compared to the Model group. WN promotes the long-term restoration of sleep and body weight in rats with wound-induced sleep disturbances. WN regulates inflammatory responses, facilitating inflammation resolution and expediting the transition to the repair phase.
