papers.title: Integrative EEG/fMRI evidence for a multi-scale network underlying self-face and personal-object recognition.
papers.abstract: The sense of ownership of our faces and possessions shapes our visual perception. While the neural basis of self-face recognition has been well-studied, the neural basis of recognizing personally owned objects remains poorly understood. The main aim of this study was to investigate brain activity underlying self-face and personal object recognition, with a particular focus on the extent to which the ownership processing can be characterized as either domain-general and/or stimulus-specific. We first review the relevant literature and then report findings from two experiments - one using EEG and the other fMRI - in which the same 30 participants categorized images of faces and objects as either "mine" or "others". EEG results revealed ownership-related visuo-midfrontal activity, reflected in event-related potentials (visual P1 and N170, and midfrontal N150 and SMN), frequency-specific inter-source phase coherence (in theta band), and brain-wide time-frequency power dynamics (in alpha, beta, and theta bands). fMRI results identified ownership-related activity in four right hemisphere regions: the inferior temporal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, and superior parietal lobule; each of which formed distinct ownership-related subnetworks. The findings support "a hybrid model" in which stimulus-specific visual pathways (e.g., face-sensitive regions) interact with domain-general frontal activity encoding self-relevance. This integrative evidence clarifies how a dynamic, multi-scale network underlying ownership perception is constructed across time, frequency, and brain space.

papers.title: Time-Restricted Ketogenic Diet Combined with Exercise Improves Cardiorespiratory Fitness but Compromises Sleep Quality in Overweight and Obese Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Obesity and sleep disorders interact bidirectionally, complicating health management. Ketogenic diets (KD) aid weight loss, but their impact on sleep quality, especially when combined with exercise, remains unclear. This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of short-term non-energy-restricted and time-restricted KD, alone or combined with moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) or sprint interval training (SIT), on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and sleep quality in overweight/obese young adults. 68 participants were randomized into CON, KD-CON, KD-SIT, and KD-MICT groups (n = 17 each), with 59 completing the 4-week intervention. Primary outcomes were peak oxygen uptake (VO₂peak) for CRF and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) for sleep quality. All KD groups achieved significant weight loss (5.0-6.0%, d = -2.5 to -1.9). Relative VO₂peak increased in KD-SIT (+13.0%, d = 1.1) and KD-MICT (+7.8%, d = 0.6) groups. However, all KD groups exhibited elevated PSQI scores (12.2-29.8%; d = 0.3-1.0), indicating impaired sleep quality. Daytime dysfunction scores fell in the KD-MICT (-31.3%, d = -0.2) and KD-SIT groups (-20.0%, d < 0.01), but rose in KD-CON (+66.7%). Greater weight loss correlated with larger increases in PSQI (r = -0.5, p < 0.01). Protocol adherence ranged from 82.4% to 94.1%. Short-term time-restricted KD reduces weight and improves CRF when combined with exercise, especially SIT, but temporarily impairs sleep quality. Exercise partially attenuated daytime dysfunction, suggesting that cardiorespiratory adaptations occur earlier than sleep-related adjustments during early KD intervention.

papers.title: Robust Detection of Major Depressive Disorder Using Empirical Mode Decomposition-Based EEG Signal Analysis.
papers.abstract: Depression is universally known as a mood disorder, which is a serious and common disease that causes moral weakness and suicidal mortality. Most psychophysiologists, sought to use physiological data to infer this psychiatric illness. This work focuses on developing a major depression disorder detection system using EEG signals. In this study, a publicly available dataset is used. 19 channels of EEG signals data are collected from 16 depressive subjects and 16 healthy subjects with closed eyes and subsequently subjected to preprocessing procedures. Using correlation coefficients and standard deviation parameters, just 14 channels are selected. The first minute recording of EEG channels is processed using empirical mode decomposition (EMD) to extract some features, which are then used for the detection of major depressive disorder (MDD). These features are extracted, first by the decomposition of EEG channels into IMFs; then by the extraction of instantaneous amplitude and instantaneous frequency of each IMF. These features show significant differences between MDD subjects and healthy subjects. Using the linear kernel of the support vector machine (SVM), the classification results achieve higher accuracy, after dimensionality reduction with the principal component analysis method. All performance measures including accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive value reach 100%. Thus, the findings confirm the robustness of the proposed system in detecting MDD.

papers.title: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation for Fibromyalgia in Veterans: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Feasibility Study of Resting-State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Evaluate Pain and Treatment Response.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans. In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function. Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred. Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

papers.title: The Mediating Effect of Sleep Quality on the Relationship Between Frailty and Cognitive Impairment Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: To investigate the relationship between physical frailty and cognitive impairment among community-dwelling older adults and the mediating role of sleep quality in that relationship. Cross-sectional study. A convenience sample of 2830 participants aged 60 years and above from Xi'an, China was assessed using the FRAIL scale, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Comprehensive data on sociodemographic and health-related covariates were collected. Statistical analyses included chi-square tests, multivariate binary logistic regression, Spearman's correlation and mediation analysis using PROCESS (Model 4) with 5000 bootstraps. The prevalence of cognitive impairment was 21.77%. Cognitive function was negatively correlated with physical frailty and sleep quality, whereas physical frailty was positively correlated with sleep quality. Age ≥ 85 years, middle school education, sleep duration > 8 h and stroke were independently associated with higher odds of cognitive impairment. Sleep quality partially mediated the frailty-cognition relationship, accounting for 12.37% of the total effect. Sleep quality partially mediates the relationship between physical frailty and cognitive impairment, highlighting a critical opportunity for nurses to implement targeted sleep hygiene interventions alongside physical frailty management to potentially mitigate cognitive decline in the growing community-dwelling geriatric population. No patient or public contribution. Nurses should incorporate routine sleep quality screening into standard geriatric health assessments, particularly for frail older adults. In community settings, nurses can take the lead in delivering targeted sleep hygiene education, coordinating multidisciplinary management for underlying sleep disorders, and tailoring interventions to match each patient's frailty severity. These findings highlight the importance of integrating sleep quality assessment into routine geriatric care. For the growing aging population, nurses working in community settings can play a critical role in delivering targeted sleep hygiene interventions and managing physical frailty to potentially help preserve older adults' cognitive function.

papers.title: Cardiovascular Health Among High School Students - Youth Risk Behavior Survey, United States, 2025.
papers.abstract: Monitoring cardiovascular health (CVH) among adolescents can identify opportunities for school and community programs to promote healthy behaviors and reduce cardiovascular disease risk. In this report, data from the nationally representative 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) of U.S. high school students were used to calculate scores for five metrics of CVH aligned with the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 framework: diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep health, and body mass index (BMI). Each of the five metrics assessed in this analysis was scored from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating more favorable levels of the corresponding metric. The five metric scores were averaged to produce an overall CVH score, with higher scores indicating a more favorable overall CVH score. Weighted mean scores and the prevalence of high (80-100), moderate (50-79), and low (0-49) scores were estimated overall and by sex, grade, and race and ethnicity.Among 5,192 students with complete data, the mean overall CVH score was 65.3; 20.7% had high, 61.3% had moderate, and 18.0% had low overall CVH scores. For the CVH metrics, mean scores were highest for BMI (85.4, reflecting lower BMI) and nicotine exposure (80.5, reflecting lower exposure), and lowest for diet (39.3), sleep health (59.1), and physical activity (62.0). The overall CVH score was lower among female (64.2) than male (66.2) students. The overall CVH score was higher for grade 9 students (68.3) than for grade 10 (65.9), 11 (63.7), and 12 (62.7) students. Compared with most other racial and ethnic groups, the overall CVH score was higher among Asian students (70.2) and lower among Black or African American students (60.2). Similar demographic patterns were observed for the prevalence of high overall CVH scores.In 2025, approximately four in five U.S. high school students had a low or moderate overall CVH score, underscoring the importance of promoting healthy adolescent behaviors, such as healthy eating, sleep, and physical activity, to support healthier trajectories into adulthood. These findings highlight opportunities to monitor and improve CVH-related behaviors and indicators among adolescents, including within school and community settings.

papers.title: Personalized assessment of high-definition slow-oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation (so-tDCS) in older adults with sleep and subjective cognitive complaints: A study protocol for a randomized clinical trial.
papers.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) is increasingly recognized as an early and potentially modifiable stage in the trajectory of neurodegenerative diseases. In older adults with SCD, untreated sleep disturbances may accelerate the neurodegenerative process, potentially via mechanisms involving amyloid-beta accumulation, and contribute to more rapid cognitive deterioration. Currently, non-pharmacological treatment options that concurrently manage SCD and sleep disturbances remain scarce. High-definition slow-oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation (so-tDCS) is an emerging, frequency-specific neuromodulation technique designed to enhance brain health and cognition. This is a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled clinical trial. Right-handed Chinese older adults with SCD and sleep disturbances will be randomly assigned to receive either high-definition 0.75 Hz so-tDCS or sham stimulation over a 4-week intervention period, with 40 participants per group. Outcome measures, including galvanic skin response, subjective cognitive complaints, sleep quality, salivary amyloid-beta levels, and domain-specific cognitive performance, will be evaluated at four time points: baseline, week 4 (immediately post‑intervention), and follow‑up at weeks 8 and 12. Personalized neurophysiological signals, namely electrode-skin impedance, will be monitored using state-of-the-art measurement during so-tDCS. The successful implement of this signal will provide researchers with access to an "add-on" setting that enables them to easily, quickly and quantitatively evaluate real-time neurophysiological signals, thereby facilitating the incorporation of transcranial brain stimulation into clinical practice. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07433738.

papers.title: Changes in clinical management related to continuous versus routine EEG in critically ill adults: analysis of a randomized trial.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) is increasingly utilized in the intensive care unit for consciousness-impaired patients with various conditions. It is, however, costly in terms of technical and human resources, and its impact on prognosis compared with routine EEG (rEEG) remains debated. We aimed to characterize the effect of cEEG vs rEEG on clinical management modifications, and to determine if these correlated with a better outcome. This is an ancillary analysis using data of CERTA (NCT03129438), a randomized trial comparing cEEG versus repeated rEEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness. Clinical management modifications due to the EEG intervention, pre-defined as performed within 60 hours of EEG start, were prospectively recorded (anti-seizure medication -ASM, sedation, new radiological examination, new surgical intervention, withdrawal of life sustaining therapy). Correlation with the EEG type were analyzed by 2x2 tables; Mantel-Haenszel tests explored the impact on mortality and functional outcome at 6 months. The trial included 364 patients completing follow-up (182 each in the cEEG and rEEG groups). While 58.2% of cEEG and 45.6% of rEEG patients had any management change (p= 0.018), ASM were modified in 22.0% (cEEG) and 12.1% (rEEG) (p = 0.012)); other clinical interventions were comparable across EEG groups. Adjusting for ASM modifications, mortality (p=0.845) and functional outcome (p=0.619) remained similar between the EEG groups. In critically ill adults, cEEG is associated with more clinical management modifications compared to repeated rEEG, particularly regarding ASM, but this does not seem to translate into improved patients' outcomes.

papers.title: Gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation prevents scopolamine-induced damage to EEG activity and spatial memory.
papers.abstract: BackgroundDementia is a serious public health concern, primarily caused by Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) can improve cognitive function by modulating neural oscillations. While tACS shows therapeutic potential for dementia, its preventive effects remain unknown. Because tACS has long-lasting modulatory effects, we propose that these offline effects may help prevent dementia.ObjectiveThis study aims to determine whether pre-administered 40 Hz tACS prevents scopolamine-induced impairment of electroencephalogram (EEG) activity and spatial cognition. Scopolamine induces cholinergic dysfunction in animal models, mimicking AD-related behavioral and EEG abnormalities.MethodsScopolamine (3 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered to induce a mouse model of dementia. Prior to induction, tACS targeting the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and/or hippocampus (Hip) was performed for five days (40 Hz, 300 μA, 20 min/day). EEG activity was recorded from the PFC and Hip during spontaneous and task-related (Y-maze) states. In addition, spatial memory was evaluated using the Barnes maze test, and general activity including locomotion and anxiety was evaluated using the open field test.ResultsScopolamine reduced spontaneous EEG activity in gamma frequency band and task-related PFC EEG activity across multiple frequency bands. Prior Hip tACS prevented these EEG reductions. Behaviorally, scopolamine induced spatial memory deficits and increased locomotion and anxiety-like behaviors. Notably, dual-site tACS reversed memory impairment and PFC tACS reduced locomotion. In addition, tACS had little effect on anxiety.ConclusionsPrior gamma tACS exerts region-specific protection against scopolamine-induced EEG and behavioral impairments, providing first evidence for its potential as a preventive strategy for dementia-related deficits.

papers.title: Designing optimal perturbation inputs for system identification in neuroscience.
papers.abstract: Investigating the dynamics of neural networks, which are governed by connectivity between neurons, is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Because passive (spontaneous) activity provides only limited information for estimating connectivity, perturbation-based approaches are widely applied in neuroscience as they can evoke underlying hidden dynamics. However, the characteristics of such perturbations have typically been designed based on empirical or biological intuition. To enable more accurate estimation of connectivity, we propose a data-driven and theoretically grounded framework for optimally designing perturbation inputs, based on formulating the neural model as a control system. The core theoretical insight underlying our approach is that neural signals observed in the passive state lack sufficient latent information, which leads to failures in the system identification. Perturbations reveal these hidden dynamics and lead to improved estimation. Guided by these insights, we derive a theoretical basis for optimizing perturbation inputs that minimize estimation errors in neural system identification. Building upon this, we further explore the relationship of this theory with stimulation patterns commonly used in neuroscience, such as frequency, impulse, and step inputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework for neuroscience through simulations grounded in experimental paradigms, such as neural state classification and optimal control of neural states. Our theoretical analysis, together with multiple simulations, consistently shows that perturbations designed according to our framework achieve substantially more accurate system identification compared to the conventional, intuition-based inputs. This study provides a theoretical foundation for designing perturbation inputs to achieve accurate estimation of neural dynamics. This, in turn, enables reliable discrimination of neural states such as levels of consciousness and pathological conditions, and facilitates precise control of their transitions toward recovery from abnormal states.

papers.title: Spatial distribution of blood-brain barrier membrane proteins is controlled by sorting motifs and physiological signals in vivo.
papers.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB), formed by brain endothelial cells (BECs), creates a safe and homeostatic environment for proper brain function. While BECs are extraordinarily thin, their luminal and abluminal plasma membranes face markedly different environments: the blood and brain parenchyma, respectively. How BBB membrane proteins are spatially distributed between these membranes and the factors regulating their localization are not clear. Here, we establish a method for measuring polarized protein sorting at the BBB in vivo. We characterize the distribution of transporters and receptors on the luminal and abluminal plasma membranes and identify protein-intrinsic motifs that control polarized sorting. Finally, we observe a change in membrane protein distribution that aligns with circadian rhythms, revealing an under-appreciated dimension of BBB dynamics. This method can be broadly used for evaluating membrane protein landscape changes during development and disease and for choosing optimal molecular targets for BBB-crossing therapeutics.

papers.title: A systemic circadian nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) signal engages the unfolded protein response and adipogenesis via the prefoldin complex.
papers.abstract: Daily light-dark cycles impose environmental fluctuations that require coordinated regulation of physiology. This coordination is mediated by the circadian clock, which operates as a network of tissue oscillators; however, the signals that convey circadian information between organs remain incompletely defined. We identify nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) as a circulating metabolite whose rhythmicity depends on the liver clock. In adipocytes and neuronal cells, NaR engages the unfolded protein response (UPR). Proteome-wide stability profiling implicates the prefoldin complex as a target of NaR, linking NaR exposure to altered proteostasis. In adipocytes, NaR-induced UPR signaling converges on the transcription factor CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha (CEBPA). Sustained NaR exposure suppresses adipocyte lipid deposition, whereas temporally restricted NaR stimulation enhances adipogenesis. Together, these findings identify NaR as a liver clock-controlled circulating metabolite that couples systemic circadian metabolism to proteostasis and tissue remodeling, revealing a mechanism by which temporal metabolic signals shape tissue-specific physiological outcomes.

papers.title: Myoclonus as a neurologic manifestation of hypoglycemia in dogs.
papers.abstract: Myoclonus consists of brief, shock-like jerks and is not reported in dogs as a neurological manifestation of hypoglycemia. To describe hypoglycemia-associated myoclonus in dogs and report diagnostic findings, treatment, and outcome. Ten dogs presenting myoclonus and concurrent hypoglycemia. Multicenter, retrospective study of dogs presenting hypoglycemia-related myoclonus. All dogs presented with myoclonus. Neurological examination was abnormal in 5/10 (50%). Myoclonus was generalized in 8/10 (80%) dogs and focal (head) in 2/10 (20%), with progression to generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizures in 5/10 (50%). Hypoglycemia (<3.3 mmol/L) was observed in all dogs (median, 2.07 mmol/L) during the myoclonic episodes. Insulinoma was a suspected (n = 1), presumptive (n = 5), or definitive (n = 3) diagnosis in 9/10 (90%) dogs. One dog (10%) developed iatrogenic hypoglycemia after IV administration of fast-acting human insulin and myoclonic episodes resolved after dose reduction. Among dogs with suspected, presumptive or confirmed insulinoma, 5/9 (56%) received medical treatment alone, 3/9 (33%) combined medical and surgical treatment, and 1/9 (11%) was not treated. Medical treatment included, prednisolone (n = 6), diazoxide (n = 3) and therapeutic diet (n = 6). Surgical treatment consisted of pancreatic mass resection. Medical or surgical treatment resulted in short-term improvement in myoclonus frequency in all dogs, however, four were later euthanized due to recurrence of hypoglycemia and myoclonus. Myoclonus might represent an underrecognized neurological manifestation of hypoglycemia in dogs. Measurement of blood glucose concentrations is a fundamental diagnostic approach for identifying hypoglycemia-related myoclonus. Treatment can lead to clinical improvement, but prognosis is dependent on the underlying cause.

papers.title: Integrative analysis of Alzheimer's disease molecular networks with circadian regulators for prioritization of drug repurposing candidates.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by complex molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence indicates that circadian rhythm disruption contributes to disease progression and interacts with pathogenic pathways. Although multi-omics resources, compound perturbation profiles, and pharmacological bioactivity data are increasingly available, their integrative use for drug repurposing prioritization in AD, particularly with explicit consideration of circadian rhythm, remains limited.ObjectiveThis study aimed to prioritize drug repurposing candidates for AD, by integrating heterogeneous biological and pharmacological data.MethodsWe applied an integrative, systems-level computational analysis to prioritize drug repurposing and repositioning candidates for AD by combining network-based gene prioritization, functional transcriptomic similarity analysis, and target-level bioactivity prediction. Disease-associated molecular modules were identified within the human protein-protein interaction network, with circadian rhythm regulators incorporated as an additional disease relevant biological context. These modules were represented using functional gene embeddings to rank compound perturbation signatures. Candidate compounds were subsequently refined through ligand-based bioactivity prediction across AD associated targets to support polypharmacological prioritization.ResultsThe analysis prioritized compounds supported by convergent network-level disease relevance, transcriptomic similarity, and predicted target engagement. Several drugs previously investigated in dementia-related clinical trials were recovered. Novel repositioning candidates, including PF-562271, MGCD-265, and BMS-777607, were identified, converging on focal adhesion kinase (FAK), PI3K-AKT, and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways enriched in AD-associated genes and implicated in circadian regulation and neuroinflammation.ConclusionsThis integrative analysis identifies mechanistically coherent repurposing candidates, associated with circadian and inflammatory pathways, supporting systems-based strategies for therapeutic prioritization in complex neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Clinical utility of additional non-absorbable nasal packing after septoplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the clinical utility of additional non-absorbable nasal packing when combined with transseptal suturing or septal splints. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted using two analytical frameworks: septal suture plus non-absorbable packing versus septal suture alone or septal suture with absorbable packing, and septal splint plus non-absorbable packing versus septal splint alone or packing alone. Outcomes of interest included postoperative bleeding, septal hematoma, adhesion/synechia formation, postoperative pain, headache, and sleep disturbance. In the suture-based analysis, additional non-absorbable packing did not significantly reduce postoperative bleeding or septal hematoma formation but was associated with higher rates of headache (odds ratio [OR]: 40.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 16.05-99.99) and synechia formation (OR: 2.79, 95% CI: 1.00-7.77). In the splint-based analysis, additional packing did not significantly reduce postoperative hemorrhage or overall adhesion rates. Although splint plus packing reduced adhesion formation compared with packing alone, no advantage was observed compared with splint-only treatment. Additional packing was also associated with significantly higher postoperative pain scores on postoperative days 1 and 7. Additional non-absorbable nasal packing after septoplasty provides no consistent clinical benefit when effective septal stabilization has already been achieved and is associated with increased postoperative discomfort. These findings do not support the routine use of additional non-absorbable nasal packing following contemporary septoplasty.

papers.title: Untapped potential: Population health co-benefits of restricting social media and smartphone use among young people.
papers.abstract: Efforts to reduce youth social media and smartphone use, including social media age restrictions and restrictions on smartphone use in schools, are increasingly being implemented in response to concerns about mental health and educational outcomes. However, evaluating these policies solely through these lenses may overlook broader population health implications. This commentary argues that digital restrictions can be viewed as upstream interventions that modify digital environments and may yield co-benefits, defined as additional favourable outcomes beyond their primary aims. Drawing on evidence linking excessive screen time and social media use with poor sleep, physical inactivity, sedentary behaviour, and unhealthy dietary patterns, we propose three pathways through which such policies may generate health co-benefits. First, restrictions may improve sleep by limiting behaviours associated with shorter and poorer-quality sleep. Second, because most recreational screen use is sedentary, restrictions may reduce sedentary time and encourage incidental physical activity. Third, they may reduce exposure to digital marketing of unhealthy foods and other harmful commodities. We also discuss equity, unintended consequences, and research gaps. Evaluating these outcomes may strengthen the evidence base for digital restrictions as one component of a comprehensive child health and chronic disease prevention strategy.

papers.title: Breastfeeding Experiences, Challenges, and Barriers Among Mothers During Hot Weather in Türkiye: A Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to explore mothers' breastfeeding experiences, challenges, and barriers during hot weather in Türkiye. A qualitative exploratory approach was used in this study. Between August and October 2024, in-depth individual interviews were conducted with mothers who applied to the breastfeeding outpatient clinic at the obstetrics and gynecology hospital in a city in the Western Black Sea region of Türkiye. The sample included 18 mothers who agreed to participate in the study. Thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. Five main themes emerged from the interviews: (1) physical and emotional barriers to breastfeeding, (2) social and privacy barriers to breastfeeding, (3) psychological challenges and support needs, (4) environmental and climatic barriers, and (5) strategies for overcoming breastfeeding barriers. The findings indicate that hot weather conditions are associated with various challenges for mothers, such as physical discomfort, emotional strain, social isolation, and sleep problems. Mothers expressed the need for adequate fluid consumption, appropriate environmental adjustments, and social support; they also highlighted the need for support to cope with the stress and psychological challenges they experience during hot weather conditions. This study shows that hot weather poses significant physical and emotional challenges to the breastfeeding process. In order for mothers to breastfeed comfortably in hot weather conditions, it is important to provide cool environments, increase fluid consumption, establish air-conditioned breastfeeding points in public spaces, expand social support groups, and provide guidance and psychological support from health professionals.

papers.title: Association of Fecal Calprotectin with Motor and Nonmotor Features in Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease and Atypical Parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: Gut inflammation and microbiota dysregulation are increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD). Fecal calprotectin, a neutrophil-derived protein and marker of intestinal inflammation, may serve as a non-invasive indicator of gut-brain axis dysfunction in parkinsonian disorders. To evaluate fecal calprotectin levels in idiopathic Parkinson's disease (IPD) and atypical parkinsonian syndromes-progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and multiple system atrophy (MSA)-and examine their relationship with motor and non-motor features. In this case-control study, 130 patients (IPD = 94, PSP = 23, MSA = 13) and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. All participants underwent detailed clinical evaluation, including the movement disorder society-unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (MDS-UPDRS), Hoehn and Yahr staging, the non-motor symptoms scale (NMSS), the Rome IV criteria for constipation, and the Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA). Fecal calprotectin (μg/g stool) was quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and correlated with clinical parameters. Mean fecal calprotectin was significantly higher in IPD and PSP than in controls ( P < 0.01), whereas MSA showed no significant difference. Elevated fecal calprotectin correlated positively with total NMSS scores ( r ≈ 0.3, P < 0.05) and inversely with MoCA scores, indicating a greater non-motor symptom burden and poorer cognitive performance. No significant correlation was observed with MDS-UPDRS motor scores. Among the NMSS domains, sleep/fatigue, mood/apathy, perceptual problems, memory, and sexual domains exhibited the strongest associations. Fecal calprotectin is elevated in IPD and PSP and is more strongly associated with non-motor than motor manifestations. These findings support intestinal inflammation as a contributor to parkinsonian pathophysiology and highlight fecal calprotectin as a potential biomarker of gut-brain axis dysfunction.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology

papers.title: Epilepsy in Children with Celiac Disease: Clinical and Electroencephalographic Characteristics and Outcomes in a Ten-Patient Case Series.
papers.abstract: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by gluten exposure in genetically predisposed individuals. Epilepsy has been reported among the neurological manifestations associated with celiac disease; however, the relationship between epilepsy and celiac disease remains incompletely understood, and their coexistence does not necessarily imply causality. This ten-patient case series describes the clinical, electroencephalographic, and follow-up characteristics of children with both epilepsy and celiac disease. Seven patients had focal epilepsy, whereas three had generalized epilepsy phenotypes, including presumed juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, presumed juvenile absence epilepsy, and sleep-related generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electroencephalography most commonly demonstrated posterior epileptiform abnormalities. Following initiation of a gluten-free diet and appropriate antiseizure medication, seizure freedom was achieved in all patients during follow-up. These findings suggest that epilepsy may occur in children with celiac disease and that favorable outcomes may be observed after dietary treatment. However, the present data should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of causality.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology

papers.title: Sensitization and Impaired Habituation of Somatosensory Evoked Potentials in Central Post-stroke Pain.
papers.abstract: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP) is associated with hyperpathia and allodynia, and neurophysiological biomarkers may help to clarify these mechanisms. We report sensitization and impaired habituation of median somatosensory evoked potentials (MSEPs) in CPSP and examine their association with quantitative sensory testing (QST) and clinico-radiological features. Thirty-four CPSP patients and 18 matched healthy controls were prospectively included. Clinical evaluation, QST, Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based stroke location were recorded. Five consecutive MSEP blocks were obtained bilaterally. N19 latency and amplitude from block 1, as well as habituation across blocks 1 to c5, were analyzed. Impaired habituation was defined as failure of amplitude reduction in blocks 2-5 compared with block 1. CPSP patients showed significantly prolonged N19 latency (21.7 ± 2.25 ms vs 18.8 ± 1.26 ms) and reduced amplitude (3.1 ± 1.57 μV vs 6.2 ± 2.58 μV) compared with controls. N19 amplitude was also reduced on the unaffected side. Tactile threshold correlated with higher pain intensity ( P = 0.04), inversely with allodynia ( P = 0.01), and with extra-thalamic lesions ( P = 0.01). Impaired habituation occurred in 64.7% of CPSP patients and was significantly associated with hyperalgesia ( P = 0.008). CPSP is marked by altered somatosensory processing, reduced cortical excitability, and impaired habituation, reflecting maladaptive thalamocortical plasticity.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology

papers.title: From spectral parameterization to spectral staging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
Decoding object categories from electroencephalography during free viewing reveals early information evolution compared to passive viewing.
papers.abstract: Object processing is central to visual perception, and its neural substrates inform cognitive and computational models of vision. Electroencephalographic (EEG) research has increasingly adopted multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode distributed neural representations, moving beyond average signal changes and predefined electrodes. Yet, most MVPA studies use passive viewing paradigms that constrain eye movements and evoke brain activity by external stimuli presentation, creating an artificial dissociation between perception and action. Here, we examine object category representations during active vision by combining MVPA with a deconvolution method for overlapping fixation-related responses. By decoding category information from single fixations, we compare the temporal dynamics of object processing between free viewing (active) and rapid serial visual presentation (passive) conditions. We find that categorical information, across multiple levels of abstraction, can be decoded from individual fixations during natural viewing, and that object representations generalize across passive and active conditions. Notably, representational dynamics time-locked to fixation onset emerge earlier than those time-locked to stimulus onset. We discuss the possibility that object processing begins parafoveally, aligned with saccade onset, rather than foveally at fixation. Thus, information about what and when to expect new information, available in free viewing, facilitates processing. These findings underscore the importance of studying vision in naturalistic settings and highlight key methodological considerations for combining MVPA with deconvolution in overlapping neural data. Object processing is fundamental to visual perception and to cognitive and computational models of vision. Although MVPA has advanced EEG research by enabling the decoding of distributed neural representations with high temporal precision, it has been applied primarily in passive viewing paradigms that constrain natural eye movements. The current study bridges the gap between passive and active vision research by combining MVPA with overlap deconvolution to decode object category information from EEG during natural fixations in free viewing. This approach reveals that category-specific representations emerge earlier in active viewing, likely reflecting processing that begins during saccade planning or execution. The findings underscore the importance of studying vision under ecologically valid conditions and introduce a novel methodological framework for capturing neural dynamics during active perception.

papers.title: BeatVecNet classifies drug-induced contractile phenotypes from beat-gated motion vectors in micropatterned human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes.
papers.abstract: Assessment of electrophysiological cardiotoxicity in vitro has advanced, yet scalable assays for contractile dysfunction remain limited. BeatVecNet, an interpretable deep-learning framework, classifies drug-induced contractile phenotypes from beat-gated motion vectors in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). BeatVecNet was developed and evaluated using beat-gated motion-vector tensors derived from hiPSC-CMs recorded by label-free phase-contrast imaging at 150 fps. hiPSC-CMs were cultured on micropatterned substrates to provide a consistent contraction axis for directional motion analysis. Dense optical flow was used to derive motion vectors, which were retained as beat-gated spatiotemporal tensors rather than reduced to scalar traces. The model uses two convolutional branches to process horizontal and vertical velocity components separately and was evaluated on independent assays containing control, doxorubicin, trastuzumab and sunitinib. BeatVecNet distinguished drug-induced contractile phenotypes with a macro-F1 of 0.916, outperforming conventional kinematic classifiers (best baseline 0.706), with the largest advantage at low doses. Branch-replacement ablation indicated non-redundant contributions of horizontal and vertical motion components, with trastuzumab classification showing greater sensitivity to horizontal-component replacement and sunitinib classification to vertical-component replacement. Phase-resolved attribution further identified temporal patterns within the beat cycle not explained by peak velocity alone. Micropatterning improved signal consistency and contractile coherence, enabling robust directional motion analysis. BeatVecNet extracts drug-associated contractile signatures not captured by conventional scalar analysis while providing direction- and phase-resolved interpretability at the motion-representation level. This platform complements electrophysiology-centred safety assessment and provides proof of concept for classification of subtle drug-induced contractile phenotypes.

papers.title: Prophylactic oral diosgenin attenuates acute sleep deprivation-induced liver injury in mice via modulation of the gut microbiota and vascular barrier.
papers.abstract: Acute sleep deprivation (SD) is an increasingly prevalent health risk, yet the early inflammatory processes associated with acute hepatic injury following SD remain largely elusive. Following a two-step screening of 265 natural products and bioactive small molecules, diosgenin (DG), a sapogenin found in Dioscorea species, was prioritized for subsequent in vivo evaluation. Under the rotating-platform paradigm in mice, 24-hour SD (SD24h) was associated with acute hepatic inflammation, increased overall intestinal permeability, gut vascular barrier (GVB)-associated alterations, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and elevated intestinal and hepatic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels. Prophylactic oral DG pretreatment attenuated hepatic and intestinal inflammatory responses, intestinal permeability changes, and GVB-associated alterations, while partially ameliorating SD-associated changes in the gut microbiota and intestinal and hepatic LPS levels. Fecal microbiota transplantation further showed that microbiota from SD24h donors transferred part of the hepato-intestinal inflammatory and barrier-associated phenotypes to antibiotic-pretreated recipients, whereas microbiota from DG-pretreated SD24h donors transferred an attenuated phenotype. Collectively, these findings support the involvement of the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier in acute SD-associated liver injury and indicate that prophylactic oral DG pretreatment attenuates these hepato-intestinal responses.

papers.title: Immediate Resumption of Positive Airway Pressure Following Sinus Surgery: A Prospective Controlled Multicenter Study.
papers.abstract: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in the perioperative period confers significant cardiopulmonary risk. However, many otolaryngologists defer restarting positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy following functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) due to perceived risk of epistaxis, mucosal injury, and wound healing. Thus, the objective of this study was to evaluate the immediate resumption of PAP therapy in OSA patients undergoing FESS. Multicenter prospective controlled study. Academic medical centers. Patients with a history of OSA on PAP therapy scheduled for FESS were prospectively enrolled (OSA/PAP group) along with a control group of non-OSA FESS patients (non-OSA group). Patients in the OSA/PAP group restarted PAP therapy on post-operative Day #0 or #1. The primary outcome was change in Lund-Kennedy endoscopic scores (LKES); secondary outcomes of interest included change in post-operative SNOT-22 scores, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores, complications, and epistaxis severity scores. A total of 100 patients were enrolled, of whom 49 were in the OSA/PAP group, and 51 were in the non-OSA group. In multivariate adjusted models, early PAP resumption was not independently associated with higher LKES compared to the control group at POV1 or POV2, higher SNOT-22 compared to the control group at POV1 or POV2, or higher postoperative epistaxis scores compared to the control group. There were no PAP-related complications such as orbital emphysema or pneumocephalus. Early resumption of PAP in OSA patients undergoing FESS does not appear to be associated with worsened post-operative endoscopic scores, quality-of-life scores, or an increased risk of post-operative epistaxis.
papers.journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery

papers.title: Stage-Specific Patterns of Imaging and Non-Motor Biomarkers in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3.
papers.abstract: Advancements in disease-modifying therapies for spinocerebellar ataxia Type 3 (SCA3) underscore the need for robust biomarkers to monitor disease progression and evaluate treatment efficacy. Although motor phenotypes have been well characterized, less is known about non-motor and imaging-based features across different disease stages. This study aimed to characterize stage-specific patterns of non-motor and imaging biomarkers in SCA3. This cross-observational study included 229 patients with SCA3 and 104 age- and sex-matched healthy controls from the Organization for Southeast China for cerebellar ataxia research. Non-motor symptoms were assessed using a battery of neuropsychological tests. Brain volume loss was assessed by 3.0-Tesla MRI with regions-of-interest (ROI)-based volumetric analysis. Neuroinflammation was quantified in vivo using translocator protein positron emission tomography (TSPO-PET) with the 18F-DPA-714 radioligand. Additive regression models were fitted to evaluate the cross-sectional associations between biomarkers and disease stages. Receiver operating curve (ROC) analyses were applied to estimate the discriminative ability of the candidate biomarkers. Non-motor symptoms, including cognitive functions, anxiety, fatigue, depression, and sleep quality, declined after ataxia onset in SCA3. Volume loss in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon diverged from normal controls at 0.7 and 0.2 years before ataxia onset, respectively. Correspondingly, the TSPO signal in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon increased and deviated from normal throughout the disease course. Our findings propose a staging model of SCA3 that includes a biomarker stage characterized by multidimensional objective indicators of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation from pre-ataxia to ataxia onset. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04010214.
papers.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

papers.title: Six-month supervised telerehabilitation combining pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release in adults with fibromyalgia: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effects of a 6-month supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation programme combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release on fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, and psychological outcomes. Two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. 68 adults with fibromyalgia confirmed according to the 2016 ACR criteria. Participants were randomized to a 6-month supervised home-based telerehabilitation programme (n = 35) or usual care (n = 33). The intervention comprised 3 live online sessions weekly combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise, self-myofascial release, core stabilization, low-load resistance exercise, stretching, and relaxation. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months using validated patient-reported measures. Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for fibromyalgia impact (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.132), sleep quality (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.129), depressive symptoms (p = 0.002, partial η2 = 0.129), and perceived stress (p = 0.028, partial η2 = 0.065), but not for anxiety (p = 0.701). Mean intervention adherence was 87.5%, with no adverse or serious adverse events reported in either group. 6 months of supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation produced favourable longitudinal changes in fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and perceived stress compared with usual care.

papers.title: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: epidemiology, pathophysiology, therapeutic strategies, and maternal-offspring outcomes.
papers.abstract: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) encompass chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and preeclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension, affecting about 5% to 10% of pregnancies worldwide and remaining a major cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Their burden is increasing with rising obesity, advanced maternal age, evolving diagnostic criteria, and marked socioeconomic and racial-ethnic disparities. This review summarises current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, biomarkers, clinical management, and long-term outcomes of HDP, highlighting recent advances and unresolved questions. Mechanistically, HDP is characterised by systemic endothelial dysfunction and angiogenic imbalance, particularly involving soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), placental growth factor (PlGF), and soluble endoglin (sEng), together with immune maladaptation, oxidative stress, and genetic and environmental contributors such as endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and sleep-disordered breathing (SDB). The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio is among the most validated tools for short-term risk assessment in suspected preeclampsia, while retinal microvascular imaging may provide a non-invasive marker of systemic microvascular dysfunction. Clinically, trial evidence supports treating mild chronic hypertension to below 140/90 mmHg to reduce adverse outcomes without compromising foetal growth. Long-term maternal cardiovascular and metabolic risks vary according to HDP phenotype, severity, gestational age at onset, and associated preterm delivery or foetal growth restriction, whereas offspring neurodevelopmental associations are largely observational and may be influenced by prematurity and shared familial or socioeconomic factors. Experimental strategies supported primarily by preclinical or early translational evidence include PPARγ agonists, placenta-targeted nanomedicine, and transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation. Machine learning combined with longitudinal multi-omics data may support precision risk stratification and individualised management.

papers.title: Biopsychosocial barriers and facilitators in the everyday lives of patients with restless legs syndrome: a qualitative study.
papers.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common condition affecting 3% of the world's population. Pharmacological treatments do not cure RLS, and symptoms substantially affect everyday life. However, knowledge of biopsychosocial (BPS) factors influencing patients' everyday lives remains limited. This study aimed to explore and describe BPS barriers and facilitators influencing everyday life among patients with RLS. A deductive, descriptive qualitative design grounded in the BPS model was employed. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted with 28 strategically selected patients from a national RLS organisation. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis and structured according to biological, psychological, and social barriers and facilitators. Biological barriers included RLS-related symptoms, sleep disturbances, and fatigue, while physical activity and environmental adaptations facilitated symptom management. Psychological barriers involved despair and inadequate healthcare responses, whereas access to information and supportive healthcare interactions enhanced everyday life. Social barriers included limitations in daily activities and the need for lifestyle adjustments. Support from patient organisations and understanding social networks facilitated coping with RLS. Together, these findings highlight how interconnected BPS factors shape patients' everyday experiences and ability to manage their condition. Comprehensive RLS care should address biological, psychological, and social barriers, particularly sleep disturbances and care-related stress, while promoting facilitating factors such as lifestyle adaptations and social support. Future research should evaluate the effects of comprehensive care interventions on symptom severity and overall BPS functioning in RLS.

papers.title: Sleep disorder and residential segregation in Cleveland, Ohio: analysis of the index of concentration at the extremes (ICE).
papers.abstract: Residential segregation is a fundamental structural determinant of health that generates social and spatial inequalities, yet its relationship with clinically diagnosed sleep disorders remains poorly understood. This study examined the association between neighborhood residential segregation and clinically diagnosed sleep disorders among 165,669 individuals residing in 265 census tracts in Cleveland, Ohio. Residential segregation was measured using the Index of Concentration at the Extremes (ICE), which captures racial segregation (ICE-Race), income segregation (ICE-Income), and racialized economic segregation (ICE-Race-Income). Logistic regression was used to estimate the odds of a sleep disorder diagnosis across quintiles of neighborhood advantage, comparing the most advantaged neighborhoods (Q5: predominantly White/highest income) with the most disadvantaged neighborhoods (Q1: predominantly Black/lowest income). In unadjusted models, residents of the most advantaged neighborhoods had significantly lower odds of a sleep disorder diagnosis than residents of the most disadvantaged neighborhoods. Specifically, individuals living in predominantly White neighborhoods had 25% lower odds of diagnosis (OR = 0.75, p < .001), those living in the highest-income neighborhoods also had 25% lower odds (OR = 0.75, p < .001), and those living in predominantly White, high-income neighborhoods had 24% lower odds (OR = 0.76, p < .001). After simultaneously adjusting for all ICE measures and individual demographic and health characteristics, only income segregation remained statistically significant, but the association reversed direction. Individuals living in the highest-income neighborhoods had 11% higher odds of a sleep disorder diagnosis than those in the lowest-income neighborhoods (OR = 1.11, p < .01). These findings suggest that the relationship between residential segregation and clinically diagnosed sleep disorders is complex and influenced by both neighborhood context and individual characteristics. The reversed association for income segregation may reflect greater healthcare access, higher screening and diagnostic rates, private insurance coverage, and potentially higher levels of social isolation in affluent neighborhoods.

papers.title: Current applications of transauricular vagus nerve stimulation in orthopedics: a narrative review of the literature.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique with emerging applications in various medical fields. While its role has been explored in neurological, psychiatric, and inflammatory conditions, its potential in orthopedics has not been reviewed in depth. Our objective was to synthesize current evidence on the use of taVNS in orthopedic conditions. A PubMed search was conducted for articles published between January 2010 and July 2025 using the terms "transcutaneous" AND "vagus nerve" AND "stimulation." Seventeen eligible studies were identified after applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Randomized controlled trials were assessed for methodological quality using the Risk of Bias 2 tool. Seventeen studies addressed the orthopedic applications of taVNS for chronic low back pain, neck pain, knee osteoarthritis, and in perioperative settings. Across the included studies, taVNS was associated with reductions in pain intensity, although superiority over control interventions was not consistent across trials; additional potential benefits were reported for sleep quality, disability indices, and psychological measures. In perioperative contexts, high-quality randomized trials demonstrated reductions in postoperative pain and analgesic requirements. However, methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and inconsistent stimulation protocols limit the strength of the conclusions. taVNS is a safe, accessible, and promising adjunctive therapy for pain management in orthopedics, with potential applications in both chronic and perioperative settings. Larger, high-quality trials are required to establish standardized protocols and clarify clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Frailty and sleep quality in elderly living in old age homes of Kathmandu Valley: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Frailty is a clinical syndrome characterized by age-related decline in strength, endurance, and physiological function that increases vulnerability to adverse health outcomes. Sleep disturbances are also common among older adults, particularly in long-term care settings, and may contribute to worsening frailty and reduced quality of life. However, limited evidence exists regarding the relationship between frailty and sleep quality among institutionalized elderly populations in Nepal. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 219 individuals aged ≥60 years residing in old-age homes in Kathmandu Valley. Participants were selected through convenience sampling. Frailty was assessed using the Groningen Frailty Indicator, and sleep quality was evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. The mean age of participants was 73.81 years (range 60-99 years), and 62.6% were female. Frailty was present in 75.3% (n = 163) of participants, with prevalence increasing from 63.5% in the 60-69 age group to 95.2% among those aged 90-99 years. Poor sleep quality was observed in 85.8% (n = 188) of participants. Among frail individuals, 95.8% had poor sleep quality. A significant association was found between frailty and poor sleep quality (r = 0.497, P < 0.001) and in adjusted analysis poor sleep quality was strongly associated with frailty (AOR = 22.58, 95% CI: 8.10-62.94, P < 0.001) . These findings highlight a strong association between frailty and poor sleep quality among elderly living in old age homes in Kathmandu valley, underscoring the need for integrated screening and management of sleep disturbances within frailty care.

papers.title: Hybrid Explainable Deep Ensemble Framework with self-attention mechanism for early prediction of depression severity using PHQ-9 clinical and behavioral data.
papers.abstract: Depression is a major global mental health disorder that requires accurate, reliable, and interpretable prediction models to support early identification and timely intervention. This study proposes a Hybrid Explainable Deep Ensemble Framework for multiclass prediction of depression severity using PHQ-9 clinical responses and behavioral characteristics. A retrospective cross-sectional machine learning study was conducted using a dataset comprising 682 anonymized participants. Predictor variables included demographic characteristics, PHQ-9 questionnaire items, sleep quality, academic pressure, and financial pressure. A hybrid ensemble integrating TabNet, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and XGBoost was developed with a self-attention mechanism for adaptive feature weighting and a weighted soft-voting strategy for final prediction. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation and an independent test set. Accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1-score, ROC-AUC, Matthews correlation coefficient, confusion matrix analysis, and SHAP-based explainability were employed to assess predictive performance and model interpretability. The proposed framework achieved an overall accuracy of 91.3%, precision of 0.907, recall of 0.898, macro F1-score of 0.902, and a macro-ROC-AUC of 0.940, outperforming the baseline machine learning models. Class-wise evaluation demonstrated the strongest performance for severe depression (F1-score = 0.934), whereas the mild depression category exhibited comparatively lower predictive performance (F1-score = 0.861) because of overlap with adjacent severity levels. Confusion matrix analysis indicated that misclassification primarily occurred between neighboring depression categories while clinically implausible predictions were rare. SHAP analysis identified sleep disturbance (PHQ-4), fatigue (PHQ-3), academic pressure, depressed mood (PHQ-2), and financial pressure as the most influential predictors. The ablation study further demonstrated that incorporating the self-attention mechanism and ensemble learning strategy improved both predictive performance and model robustness. The proposed Hybrid Explainable Deep Ensemble Framework combines high predictive accuracy with transparent decision-making for multiclass depression severity assessment. By integrating deep learning, ensemble learning, self-attention, and explainable artificial intelligence, the framework provides accurate and clinically interpretable predictions and represents a promising approach for future clinical decision-support systems and precision mental health screening.

papers.title: Trait anxiety selectively amplifies reward learning under uncertainty, while N3 sleep attenuates it.
papers.abstract: Adaptive learning under uncertainty requires distinguishing random variability (stochasticity) from true environmental change (volatility), yet how trait anxiety and sleep together influence it remains unclear. Across two preregistered experiments, participants completed a probabilistic reversal-learning task that independently manipulated volatility and stochasticity. Hierarchical Bayesian modeling showed that in stable but noisy environments, individuals with higher trait anxiety appeared to treat stochastic fluctuations as indicators of genuine change, resulting in over updating and lower evidence accumulation, while preserving normative trends in volatile environments. In a second experiment combining task performance with overnight sleep electroencephalography, greater N3 sleep was associated with reduced updating and higher evidence accumulation in stable environments among individuals with higher trait anxiety. These findings suggest that trait anxiety selectively alters how uncertainty is computationally represented, while N3 sleep appears to attenuate it. Together, these findings provide a computational framework linking anxiety, sleep, and adaptive learning under uncertainty.

papers.title: Irritable bowel syndrome and restless legs syndrome: a narrative review of epidemiological and pathophysiological overlap.
papers.abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and restless legs syndrome (RLS) are chronic, multifactorial disorders that have considerable impact on quality of life and common comorbidity with mood and sleep disorders. The present narrative review consolidates existing literature to examine the epidemiological connection, shared pathophysiological mechanisms, and clinical implications of IBS-RLS comorbidity. A literature search was conducted using PubMed and Google Scholar (2015-2025). The inclusion criteria were adult population and peer-reviewed, full-text studies on co-occurrence or mechanism between RLS and IBS. There were 48 included articles after independent screening. Observational studies report RLS prevalence in IBS patients of about 10-46%, compared with 3-14% in controls, indicating a likely bidirectional association. Both conditions share risk factors like female sex, psychiatric comorbidity, and autonomic dysfunction, and overlap in mechanisms including iron deficiency, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter imbalance, gut-brain axis disruption, and microbial dysbiosis. This supports a neurogastroenterological link and suggests shared etiologic pathways, highlighting the value of routine reciprocal screening to improve diagnosis and quality of life. The co-occurrence of IBS and RLS underscores the necessity of increased clinical vigilance and combined care. Shared mechanisms increase the potential for specific therapy approaches, including dopaminergic drugs, iron supplementation, microbiota modifications, and mast cell stabilizers. Further longitudinal and mechanistic studies are needed to clarify causality and evaluate potential dual-purpose interventions, as current evidence is largely observational and limits causal inference.

papers.title: Association between Cardiovascular Health by Life's Essential 8 and Subsequent Coronary Artery Calcium Score: The Cardiovascular and Metabolic Diseases Etiology Research Center Cohort.
papers.abstract: Although "Life's Essential 8" (LE8) is a key metric for cardiovascular health (CVH), its longitudinal association with subclinical atherosclerosis in Koreans remains unclear. We examined the association between baseline LE8 scores and the presence of coronary artery calcium (CAC). Data were obtained from the Cardiovascular and Metabolic Diseases Etiology Research Center cohort study, a prospective cohort (baseline: 2013-2018; follow-up: 2022-2024). Baseline CVH scores, comprising 8 metrics (diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep health, body mass index, blood lipids, blood glucose, and blood pressure), were categorized as low (0-<50), moderate (50-<80), and high (80-100). The main outcome was the presence of CAC at the follow-up. Multivariable logistic regression was used for statistical analysis. During a mean follow-up of 7.3 years, among 1,746 participants (mean age: 52.3 years, 65.2% female), the overall prevalence of CAC was 41.4%, which decreased with increasing CVH scores (low: 64.6%, moderate: 41.5%, and high: 30.4%). Compared to the low CVH group, the fully adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) for the presence of CAC were 0.34 (0.23-0.51) in the moderate and 0.25 (0.15-0.39) in the high CVH group. Higher baseline CVH scores were log-linearly associated with lower odds of CAC presence, demonstrating a linear and dose-dependent relationship in the restricted cubic spline plot (p = 0.102). The association between CVH and CAC was consistently observed across subgroups and sensitivity analyses. Our study showed that higher baseline CVH scores were associated with a lower risk of subsequent CAC, highlighting the importance of promoting ideal CVH early to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease.

papers.title: Respiratory failure nurse consultant model may decrease hospital days for acute respiratory failure: A single-centre descriptive implementation study.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive ventilation has become a well-established treatment for both acute and chronic respiratory failure. With the potential of telemonitoring, the use of non-invasive ventilation has improved the possibilities of treating chronic respiratory failure without physical contact with patients. The aim of this study was to describe the implementation and activities of a consulting respiratory nurse model and to estimate its potential direct budget impact based on predefined assumptions. A University hospital in Finland. All consecutive patients requiring non-invasive ventilation initiation or setting adjustment in non-pulmonary wards. Most of these patients had acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. The underlying diagnoses included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea. Patients with chronic respiratory failure due to neuromuscular diseases were excluded. This was a single-centre descriptive implementation study conducted in a Finnish university hospital. We implemented a consulting respiratory failure nurse model, whose main tasks were non-invasive ventilation initiation and follow-up visits in non-pulmonary hospital wards, consultations by phone, wireless telemonitoring of patients in non-pulmonary hospital wards and all discharged patients including those initiating non-invasive ventilation in pulmonary wards, counselling patients by phone, and replacement of a broken or unsuitable mask or device for outpatients.Data on activities of a consulting respiratory failure nurse were prospectively collected from 2019 to 2022. The direct budget impact was estimated based on changes in the estimated number of in-hospital days derived from the average hospital stay per patient, patient fees, costs of salaries, and telemonitoring licenses. A total of 240 patients initiated non-invasive ventilation in non-pulmonary wards during 2019-2022. Initiating non-invasive ventilation in non-pulmonary wards with the help of respiratory failure nurse and replacing in-hospital follow-up visits with wireless telemonitoring, home oximetry and capillary blood gas analyses, associated with an estimated potential net budget impact per patient per year of 466.57 €, 1017.35 €, 1233.80 € and 1219.67 € in year 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022, respectively. The number of overnight follow-up visits in pulmonary ward among patients initiating non-invasive ventilation decreased by 61 % during the study period. Updating the standard operating procedure for respiratory failure patients using the consulting respiratory failure nurse model and wireless telemonitoring was associated with improved care delivery and estimated potential reduction in-hospital days and direct costs.
papers.journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

papers.title: Sleep deprivation impairs ventral hippocampus-medial prefrontal connectivity and task learning in rats.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for memory consolidation, and sleep loss has long been associated with cognitive impairment. However, the circuit-level mechanisms through which sleep deprivation disrupts hippocampal-prefrontal communication during learning remain poorly understood. Here, we combined a T-maze learning task with simultaneous local field potential (LFP) recordings in the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of rats. Using dynamic causal modeling (DCM), we quantified directional connectivity during task acquisition under normal and sleep-deprived conditions. We found that learning strengthened forward connectivity from vHPC to mPFC while weakening backward connectivity from mPFC to vHPC. Sleep deprivation impaired this forward connectivity, resulting in slower learning and reduced task accuracy. These findings characterize the altered circuit dynamics by which sleep loss disrupts hippocampal-prefrontal circuit dynamics, providing insight into how impaired cross-regional communication may underlie cognitive deficits observed in sleep-related psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: The effect of macular carotenoids and omega-3 supplementation on performance in precision sports: the sport nutrition intervention in performance exercise (SNIPE) study.
papers.abstract: Macular carotenoids improve visual performance in healthy individuals, but these benefits have yet to be tested on athletes. The SNIPE study examined how the macular carotenoids [lutein (L), zeaxanthin (Z), meso-zeaxanthin (MZ)] with omega-3 fatty acids (ω3) impact visual functions and sports performance in precision sports. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 67 athletes and players randomly received either an active supplement containing L, Z, MZ + ω3 (the formulation), or a placebo containing sunflower oil over a 9 month period. Key measurements included blood serum L, Z and MZ concentrations, skin carotenoid score (SCS), visual acuity (VA) and contrast sensitivity (CS), subjective visual function, sleep health (SH), and sport specific performance tests during simulated competitions. Results showed that the active group, compared to placebo, exhibited statistically significant improvements in L (88%), Z (107%), MZ (0 to 0.226 μmol/L) blood concentrations, SCS (25%), CS at 6 cpd during dim condition (p = 0.008, η2 = 0.141), and SH in archery (p = 0.023, η2 = 0.242) and Egame (p = 0.041, η2 = 0.237). Sports performance also improved for the active group, including total shooting score of 60 shots (p = 0.047, η2 = 0.081) for shooters and archers, and simple motor time (p = 0.018, η2 = 0.302) and a suggestive trend toward faster choice reaction time (p = 0.054, η2 = 0.213) for Egame players, when compared to the placebo group. The study provides novel evidence that supplementing with carotenoids and omega-3 fatty acids enhances visual function and sports performance in precision sport athletes and players. Further research should attempt to identify the exact mechanisms by which these nutrients are enhancing visual function. These findings highlight the opportunity to add these complementary bioactive nutrients of the eye and brain to athletes' diets to help achieve peak performance in sports. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN18761383, ISRCTN18761383.

papers.title: Association between ensuring a daily rest period in the workplace and workers' sleep: Evidence from a matched employer-employee survey in Japan.
papers.abstract: This study examined how ensuring a daily rest period (DRP) in the workplace was associated with workers' sleep and whether workplace-level DRPs moderated the association between working hours and sleep, with the exploratory aim of identifying potential differences based on gender. Using cross-sectional data from a matched employer-employee survey, this study analyzed a sample consisting of 4202 full-time workers from 2121 workplaces. Logistic regression models were employed to predict sleep quantity and quality outcomes. There was no significant association between ensuring a DRP in the workplace and short sleep duration among full-time workers. Increasing working hours was significantly associated with higher odds of short sleep duration; however, this association appeared weaker among workers in workplaces with ≥11 h DRP. Exploratory analyses stratified by gender suggested that this pattern appeared more evident among women than among men. Moreover, ensuring ≥11 h DRP was significantly associated with lower odds of short sleep duration among overtime workers and daytime sleepiness among full-time workers. Gender-specific differences in insufficient sleep, early morning awakening, daytime sleepiness, and nonrestorative sleep were observed. The findings suggest the relevance of introducing a work-interval system or taking measures to ensure a DRP in the workplace for workers' sleep health. Nevertheless, further longitudinal, interventional, or quasi-experimental studies are required to establish the causal relationship between ensuring a DRP and sleep outcomes.

papers.title: Association of a 'three meals and sleep routine' lifestyle intervention with weight and metabolic health in children with obesity: a prospective, single-arm pilot study.
papers.abstract: Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment is the foundation of pediatric obesity care, but sustained adherence and weight-loss maintenance remain difficult. Regular meal and sleep timing may complement standard care, although pediatric interventional evidence is limited. This prospective, single-arm pilot study aimed to evaluate longitudinal changes in weight, body composition, and metabolic markers during a 'three meals and sleep routine' (TMSR) intervention. This prospective, single-center, single-arm pilot study consecutively included 119 children with obesity aged 5-18 years [body mass index (BMI)-for-age Z-score (BAZ) >2] from January 2022 to December 2023. Families received nutritionist-led written guidance for three structured meals per day, no caloric intake between meals, age-based energy targets of 1,500-2,300 kcal/day, a protocol-defined minimum of 7.5 hours of nighttime sleep with lights off by 22:30, and maintenance of habitual physical activity. Follow-up was planned at approximately 2-month intervals but occurred according to clinical availability. Anthropometry, bioelectrical-impedance body composition, and fasting metabolic markers were assessed. Adherence, dietary intake, sleep, and physical activity were not objectively monitored. Generalized linear mixed models used available repeated measurements to estimate average within-cohort change over time. The cohort had a mean age of 10.24±2.33 years; 82 participants (68.9%) were male and 37 (31.1%) were female. The fitted BMI trajectory decreased from approximately 26.0 kg/m2 at baseline to 24.5 kg/m2 at month 4, then increased to 25.4 kg/m2 by month 12. BAZ followed the same pattern, decreasing from 2.9 to 2.3 before increasing to 2.4. Visceral fat area and percentage body fat also declined through month 4 and subsequently rebounded. Fasting insulin and glucose showed early declines followed by partial rebound, whereas triglycerides and serum uric acid declined across follow-up. In linear-time models, average monthly coefficients were negative for BMI, BAZ, visceral fat area, percentage body fat, fasting insulin, glucose, triglycerides, and serum uric acid. These coefficients summarize within-cohort associations and do not capture the observed nonlinear trajectories. In this uncontrolled cohort, several anthropometric and metabolic measures improved during the first 4-6 months, but BMI, BAZ, adiposity measures, insulin, and glucose later showed partial rebound.
