The findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating; the absence of a comparator and objective adherence data precludes causal attribution to TMSR and limits assessment of durability and safety. Controlled, multicenter studies with age-appropriate sleep targets and objective behavioral monitoring are needed.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Pain Threshold Index-Guided Remifentanil Titration During Laparoscopic Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: To determine whether remifentanil titration guided by the pain threshold index (PTi), an electroencephalography-derived proxy for nociceptive tolerance rather than subjective pain, reduces intraoperative remifentanil infusion during laparoscopic abdominal surgery. In this prospective, single-center, assessor-blinded randomized trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery with propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion were assigned 1:1 to PTi-guided or conventional hemodynamic-guided remifentanil titration. The primary endpoint was intraoperative remifentanil infusion rate. The principal analysis used the full-analysis set and covariate-adjusted linear regression with heteroskedasticity-consistent robust standard errors. Among 200 randomized patients, 195 were analyzed (98 PTi-guided; 97 control). The primary endpoint was neutral: mean (SD) remifentanil infusion rate was 7.44 (1.43) versus 7.63 (1.41) µg kg-1 h-1; adjusted mean difference, -0.06 µg kg-1 h-1 (95% CI, -0.44 to 0.32; P=0.758). Per-protocol results were similar. Median (IQR) NRS at post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) admission was 2.0 (2.0-3.0) versus 3.0 (2.0-4.0), and Ramsay score was 2.0 (2.0-2.0) in both groups. In exploratory secondary analyses, rescue opioid was used in the PACU by 18/98 (18.4%) versus 31/97 (32.0%) patients and any rescue opioid through 48 h by 29/98 (29.6%) versus 44/97 (45.4%). Any postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) through 48 h occurred in 17/98 (17.3%) versus 29/97 (29.9%) patients. Total postoperative opioid exposure through 48 h was not reduced. PTi-guided remifentanil titration did not reduce intraoperative remifentanil infusion. PACU pain and sedation scores were not materially different. Lower early rescue-opioid use and fewer PONV events through 48 h were exploratory secondary findings, were not accompanied by lower postoperative opioid dose, and require prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Management of Post-heart Transplant Atrial Fibrillation.
papers.abstract: AF is the most common atrial arrhythmia encountered after orthotopic heart transplantation, with distinct pathophysiology and clinical implications. While early postoperative AF is typically transient, late-onset AF is increasingly recognised as a marker of graft dysfunction, rejection or vasculopathy. Risk factors include advanced recipient age, prolonged ischaemic time and immunosuppressive therapy. The denervated status of the transplanted heart alters typical electrophysiology, complicating diagnosis and management. Management requires individualised strategies balancing rate versus rhythm control, careful drug interaction monitoring and thromboembolic risk assessment. Emerging evidence supports catheter ablation in select cases, although data remain limited. Immunosuppressants, particularly calcineurin inhibitors and azathioprine, may increase AF susceptibility. Given the lack of transplant-specific AF guidelines, a multidisciplinary approach is essential. Improved understanding of AF in orthotopic heart transplantation is critical to optimising graft longevity and patient survival. Future studies are needed to guide evidence-based management and surveillance.

papers.title: Visual cues in MI-BCI induce biases in EEG classification models with deep learning but not with standard machine learning.
papers.abstract: Deep learning classification methods are increasingly popular in the brain-computer interface (BCI) field due to their ability to learn complex, non-linear representations from EEG data. Unlike traditional machine learning approaches, which typically rely on hand-crafted features, deep learning models autonomously extract spatio-temporal features directly from the raw or minimally preprocessed signal. However, this flexibility may come at the cost of reduced interpretability and increased susceptibility to confounding factors. This study aims to investigate whether the inclusion of task-related visual cues in the input EEG window biases deep learning models by leading them to exploit irrelevant features, thereby compromising their neurophysiological validity. This study investigates how including EEG signals measured during visual cue presentation on classification accuracy and feature extraction in motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs. Three classification pipelines were evaluated: CSP+LDA, a traditional machine learning approach; DeepConvNet, a convolutional neural network for EEG classification; and REVE, a Transformer-based EEG foundation model. All methods are trained and tested on two large scale open-access EEG datasets using two epoching strategies, with or without including the visual cue onset, to assess their impact on model performance and neurophysiological relevance. Attribution maps (e.g., Saliency maps) and CSP patterns are used to interpret the features learned by each model. Including the visual cue onset significantly improved the classification accuracy of DeepConvNet and REVE. However, attribution analysis showed that the model mainly relied on early parietal activations, most likely cue-related visual evoked potentials, rather than MI-related sensorimotor rhythms (ERD/ERS), which were more prominent when the cue onset was excluded. In contrast, CSP+LDA showed minimal accuracy changes across conditions, with consistent motor cortex activation patterns. These findings demonstrate that higher classification performance does not necessarily imply neurophysiological validity. In particular, deep learning models may exploit confounding signals, such as visual cue processing, which undermines their interpretability and applicability in asynchronous or real-world BCIs, in which there is no such cue. We advocate for systematically applying explainability tools in BCI research to ensure classifiers rely on task-relevant brain activity. Additionally, we emphasize the importance of excluding visual cue periods from EEG segments containing reposenses evoked by the visual cue onset from the input to deep learning models.

papers.title: Posterior segment imaging clues to systemic malignancy: a phenotype-to-confirmation narrative review.
papers.abstract: Systemic malignancies may affect the posterior segment through metastatic, paraneoplastic, hematologic or lymphomatous, and treatment-related mechanisms. Because routine ophthalmic imaging rarely establishes the underlying etiology, its principal clinical value is to identify suspicious patterns, prioritize competing diagnoses, and guide further investigation. This narrative review synthesizes malignancy-related posterior segment findings and proposes a clinically oriented phenotype-to-confirmation framework for multimodal interpretation. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for publications from January 2000 to May 18, 2026. The review included choroidal metastasis, paraneoplastic retinopathies and choroidopathies, vitreoretinal lymphoma, hematologic infiltration, leukemic retinopathy, and anticancer therapy-related toxicity. Owing to heterogeneity in disease entities, imaging protocols, diagnostic confirmation, and study designs, the evidence was synthesized qualitatively. Findings were organized into five suspicion-triggering phenotypes: exudative choroidal mass, RPE-choroidal remodeling, vitreoretinal infiltrative, diffuse neuroretinal dysfunction, and treatment-imprint phenotypes. Each phenotype was linked to its principal mimickers and to appropriate additional investigations, including targeted multimodal imaging, electrophysiology, ocular-fluid analysis, molecular testing, or systemic oncologic reassessment. These phenotypes should not be regarded as validated diagnostic categories, but as clinical entry points for differential exclusion and diagnostic escalation. Artificial intelligence may eventually support image registration, lesion tracking, and longitudinal comparison; however, its role in these rare and heterogeneous disorders remains investigational.

papers.title: Genetic susceptibility and neuroprotective gene therapy of normal tension glaucoma: a review.
papers.abstract: Normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) is a distinct form of glaucomatous optic neuropathy characterized by progressive retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration and visual field loss despite intraocular pressure (IOP) remaining within the statistically normal range. Although IOP reduction remains the only established disease-modifying strategy, continued disease progression despite adequate IOP control highlights the importance of IOP-independent mechanisms. Increasing evidence implicates vascular dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, neuroinflammation, axonal transport abnormalities, and circadian dysregulation in increased RGC vulnerability. Genetic studies have identified OPTN and TBK1 as the most strongly supported NTG-associated susceptibility genes, whereas many other candidate genes, including MYOC, SARM1, DLK, BDNF, NOS3, KLF2 and PTGDS, are shared with other glaucoma subtypes or remain supported primarily by experimental or mechanistic evidence. These interconnected processes converge on mitochondrial impairment, axonal degeneration, and RGC death, providing potential therapeutic targets beyond conventional IOP lowering. This review integrates the vascular, mitochondrial, and neuronal mechanisms underlying NTG, distinguishes NTG-associated molecular factors from pathways shared across glaucoma subtypes, and summarizes emerging gene- and nucleic-acid-based therapeutic strategies. By linking evidence-based mechanisms with emerging molecular technologies, this review provides a framework for mechanism-based and precision-oriented therapies that may complement established IOP-lowering treatment for NTG.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes following a traditional Chinese medicine foot bath preparation for lower-limb edema and sleep disturbance: a single-center retrospective study of 2,000 patients.
papers.abstract: To evaluate clinical outcomes and documented adverse events following treatment with a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) foot bath preparation in patients with lower-limb edema and sleep disturbance. This single-center retrospective observational study included 2,000 patients treated at Lanzhou Second People's Hospital between May 2017 and May 2022. All patients had varying degrees of lower-limb edema, peripheral circulatory dysfunction, and sleep disturbance. Patients received a standardized TCM foot bath preparation consisting of stir-fried peach kernel (10 g), bush cherry seed (15 g), Chinese angelica root (10 g), and safflower (10 g). The preparation was administered once daily for 20 sessions, comprising two consecutive 10-day treatment courses. Clinical outcomes were assessed by comparing ankle circumference, ABI, and PSQI values before and after treatment. Using the routine record-based classification, 1,120 patients (56.0%) were classified as "markedly effective," 770 (38.5%) as "effective," and 110 (5.5%) as "ineffective." The combined proportion was 94.5%; however, this classification is not internationally validated and is reported descriptively rather than as evidence of effectiveness. After treatment, ankle circumference and PSQI scores were significantly lower than baseline values (both P < 0.01), whereas ABI values were significantly higher (P < 0.05). Mild local adverse reactions, including transient redness and dryness, were observed in a small proportion of patients. In this single-center retrospective observational study, post-treatment changes were observed in lower-limb edema, peripheral circulation, and sleep quality.

papers.title: Can we predict who hurts most after pediatric adenotonsillectomy?
Institutional readiness to deliver total intravenous anaesthesia for obstetric patients: a national Irish survey.
papers.abstract: Total intravenous anaesthesia is a core safety standard for absolute indications, such as malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, yet little is known about institutional readiness to deliver total intravenous anaesthesia for obstetric patients. We conducted a national cross-sectional service evaluation of all 19 Irish maternity units via the Irish Society of Obstetric Anaesthesia network. Responses were received from 13/19 units, representing over 80% of the national birth activity. Most units (8/13) reported reliable access to target-controlled infusion pumps and processed electroencephalography monitoring (12/13), but 5/13 had fewer than one target-controlled infusion pump per obstetric theatre and 4/13 lacked an immediate backup pump. No unit had a written protocol for obstetric total intravenous anaesthesia, and 7/13 reported no resident training. Reported total intravenous anaesthesia use for obstetric general anaesthesia was low (0% in 8/13 units). Lack of exposure (11/13) and institutional preference for volatile agents (10/13) were the most common barriers. Readiness to deliver total intravenous anaesthesia for obstetric patients without delay is variable across Irish maternity units. Given that total intravenous anaesthesia remains mandatory in certain high-risk patient groups, including those susceptible to malignant hyperthermia, deficiencies in equipment redundancy, monitoring, training and governance are patient safety concerns which should be addressed.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic complexity and cognitive decline: Insights from approximate entropy across aging and dementia.
papers.abstract: Physiological aging involves gradual modifications of brain activity patterns sometimes leading to pathological outcomes. Understanding changes in brain signal complexity from healthy aging to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) may provide insights into cognitive decline and support early diagnosis. Electroencephalography (EEG) data were collected from 269 participants divided into three groups: healthy elderly (HE, n = 109), MCI (n = 75), and AD (n = 85). Approximate entropy (ApEn) was computed for the total EEG spectrum and frequency bands. A random forest classifier with a one-versus-one strategy and recursive feature elimination (RFE) was used for group discrimination. Additionally, group comparisons and correlations with neuropsychological scores were performed to further investigate the functional relevance of these entropy changes by assessing their association with cognitive and functional performance. Significant group differences in total ApEn were found, particularly in central brain regions, with progressive decreases from HE to MCI and AD. Frequency-specific patterns emerged: (1) delta ApEn was increased in those with AD across the scalp; (2) alpha 1 ApEn showed frontal decreases and occipital increases in the AD group, with an intermediate pattern in MCI; (3) gamma ApEn was markedly reduced in those with AD compared to both HE and MCI groups, with central and frontal localization, and extended occipital differences in those with MCI versus AD. The classifier achieved 66.55% accuracy, with sensitivities of 78.90% (HE), 49.33% (MCI), and 65.88% (AD). Positive correlations were found between ApEn and cognitive scores in both the total EEG spectrum and gamma band; conversely, delta and alpha 1 ApEn showed negative correlations with cognitive and functional scores. The distinct entropy patterns observed across frequency bands and scalp/brain regions may help characterize electrophysiological changes associated with cognitive decline and AD.

papers.title: Efficacy and neural mechanisms of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for chronic insomnia: a study protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Traditional auricular therapy for chronic insomnia (Bu Mei in TCM) is used in clinical practice but is limited by insufficient standardization and poorly understood mechanisms. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) provides a quantifiable and reproducible neuromodulatory approach by stimulating vagally innervated regions of the auricular concha, which overlap with auricular acupoints used in TCM. However, evidence in insomnia remains predominantly based on clinical outcomes, whereas longitudinal neuroimaging evidence is limited. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) may complement clinical assessments by characterizing spontaneous brain activity and treatment-related functional changes, thereby providing objective neuroimaging evidence relevant to the potential mechanisms of taVNS. This protocol will recruit 60 patients with chronic insomnia disorder (CID) and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Patients with CID will be randomized 1:1 to receive 4 weeks of active or sham-taVNS. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) will be performed at baseline in all participants and repeated at Week 4 in patients with CID, within 24 hours after the final intervention session. Fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) will serve as a prespecified exploratory neuroimaging measure, with amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) included as a complementary exploratory measure. The neuroimaging analyses will examine baseline differences between patients with CID and HCs and between-group differences in baseline-to-Week-4 changes between the active and sham-taVNS groups to characterize brain functional alterations associated with CID and changes associated with active taVNS relative to sham-taVNS. The primary clinical outcome will be the change in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score from baseline to Week 4. Secondary and follow-up assessments will evaluate insomnia severity, daytime sleepiness, emotional status, cognitive function, pre-sleep arousal, and quality of life. Exploratory correlations between changes in neuroimaging measures and clinical outcomes will also be examined. This study will integrate clinical assessments with rs-fMRI to evaluate the clinical effects of taVNS in patients with CID and explore associated changes in spontaneous brain activity. The integration of clinical outcomes and exploratory neuroimaging measures may provide complementary evidence on treatment effects and associated brain functional changes, thereby informing future investigation of the potential neural mechanisms of taVNS in CID. https://www.chictr.org.cn/hvshowprojectEN.html?id=277442&v=1.0, identifier ChiCTR2500103157.

papers.title: Applying the MANifest Health Theory to Male Firefighter Lifestyle: A Conceptual Review Using the FANTASTIC Lifestyle Assessment.
papers.abstract: Firefighters face substantial long-term health risks related to cardiovascular disease, sleep disruption, occupational stress, inconsistent preventive care, and lifestyle behaviors shaped by fire-service culture. Although firefighter health research has traditionally emphasized acute injury, sudden cardiac events, toxic exposures, and psychological trauma, less attention has been given to the broader lifestyle patterns through which chronic risk accumulates in both volunteer and career firefighters. This conceptual review argues that firefighter lifestyle should be understood as a men's health issue shaped not only by individual behavior, but also by masculinity-linked role expectations, peer culture, organizational support, stigma, and the perceived legitimacy of self-care. The MANifest Health Theory is proposed as a useful framework for interpreting these dynamics because it centers the interaction of identity, social role, environment, and preventive health behavior. The FANTASTIC Lifestyle Assessment is further proposed as a practical multidimensional tool for operationalizing firefighter lifestyle within this framework. This paper advances a firefighter-specific conceptual model and outlines implications for research, prevention, and nurse-led men's health practice.

papers.title: Effects of Nurse-Led Interventions on Adherence and Clinical Outcomes Among Adults Receiving Noninvasive Ventilation: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
papers.abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is a cornerstone therapy for respiratory diseases, but its effectiveness depends on patient adherence, which remains suboptimal. Although nurses play a key role in NIV management, the effects of nurse-led interventions on adherence and clinical outcomes remain unclear. To evaluate the effects of nurse-led interventions on NIV adherence and clinical outcomes in adults. Six databases were searched from inception to January 2026 for English randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults receiving NIV. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection and data extraction. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias 2 tool, and the findings were synthesized without meta-analysis. Sixteen RCTs involving 1757 participants were included. Risk of bias ranged from low to high across studies. Interventions included health education, motivational and behavioral strategies, and follow-up support delivered face-to-face, by telephone, or via telehealth. Nurse-led interventions may improve NIV adherence, although the effects varied across intervention types and follow-up periods. Some studies reported improvements in symptom burden, emotional status, and selected health service outcomes, whereas findings on quality of life, self-efficacy, and healthcare utilization were inconsistent. Nurse-led interventions may improve NIV adherence, particularly when combining education with motivational and behavioral strategies and structured follow-up.

papers.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of non-pharmacological interventions in improving psychological status and sleep quality among hemodialysis patients.
papers.abstract: Patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) experience substantial physical and psychological burdens. Non-pharmacological interventions have been increasingly explored as potential approaches for improving psychological symptoms and sleep quality in this population. To systematically evaluate the effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depression, anxiety, and sleep quality in patients receiving MHD. Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, CINAHL Complete, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from January 2000 to February 2026 for English-language randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool was used to assess the risk of bias in included trials. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used as effect estimates for continuous outcomes. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence. Meta-analyses were performed using RevMan 5.4 and R version 4.5.2. Fourteen randomized controlled trials were included. Meta-analyses comprised 9 studies (570 participants) for depression, 11 studies (647 participants) for anxiety, and 14 studies (871 participants) for sleep quality. Compared with usual care, non-pharmacological interventions significantly improved depression (SMD = -0.62, 95% CI: -0.87 to -0.37, I2 = 52%), anxiety (SMD = -0.86, 95% CI: -1.23 to -0.49, I2 = 79%), and sleep quality (SMD = -0.94, 95% CI: -1.33 to -0.55, I2 = 87%). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses did not materially reduce heterogeneity for anxiety or sleep quality. Exploratory subgroup analyses revealed no statistically significant differences in effect estimates according to intervention type or duration (P > 0.05). Potential publication bias was suggested for depression, whereas no statistically significant evidence of publication bias was identified for anxiety or sleep quality. Based on the GRADE framework, the certainty of evidence was moderate for depression and low for anxiety and sleep quality. The available evidence suggests that non-pharmacological interventions may improve depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and sleep quality in patients receiving MHD. However, the certainty of evidence was low for anxiety and sleep quality outcomes and moderate for depressive symptoms, and these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Identifier CRD420261370746.

papers.title: Association of healthy sleep patterns with incident cervical disc disorders: a prospective study.
papers.abstract: There is limited evidence regarding the relationship between multidimensional sleep behaviors and incident cervical disc disorders. This study examined whether a composite healthy sleep pattern was associated with the subsequent risk of cervical disc disorders. This prospective cohort study used data from the UK Biobank. Participants with baseline cervical disc disorders or missing data were excluded, leaving 399,862 participants for analysis. A composite healthy sleep score was derived from five sleep characteristics: sleep chronotype, sleep duration, insomnia, snoring, and daytime sleepiness. The primary outcome was incident cervical disc disorders, identified using ICD-10 codes (M50). Cox proportional hazards models were fitted with adjustment for demographic, lifestyle, and socioeconomic covariates. During follow-up, 2,735 incident cases were documented. Each 1-point increase in the healthy sleep score was associated with an 18% lower risk (HR = 0.82; 95% CI: 0.79-0.85). Participants with a score of 5 had a lower risk than those with a score of 0-1 (HR = 0.43; 95% CI: 0.35-0.52). The inverse association was stronger among participants with higher socioeconomic deprivation (P for interaction = 0.018). In this cohort analysis, baseline adherence to healthy sleep behaviors was associated with a significantly lower risk of cervical disc disorders, suggesting that promoting healthy sleep may be a viable strategy for primary prevention.

papers.title: Distribution and factors associated with refractive errors among young adults attending ophthalmic clinics in Iraq: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To describe the clinic-based distribution of myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism among young Iraqi adults and to examine demographic, social, familial, and self-reported behavioral factors associated with myopia and high-severity refractive errors. This multicenter, clinic-based, cross-sectional study included 4,340 consecutive young adult attendees at three tertiary ophthalmic centers. Right-eye sphere and cylinder values were standardized to minus-cylinder notation before spherical equivalent (SE), and refractive outcomes were derived. Subgroup percentages were calculated using the relevant subgroup denominator, and multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate associated factors. In the analytic sample, myopia (SE ≤ -0.50 D) occurred in 51.2%, hyperopia (SE ≥ +0.50 D) in 37.0%, and astigmatism (|cylinder| ≥ 0.50 D) in 66.4%; astigmatism overlapped with spherical refractive status. Myopia was more frequent among women than men (53.6% vs 45.6%). In the adjusted model, female sex, age 28-32 years, a positive family history of refractive error, sleep duration ≤6 hours, and longer daily electronic-device use were associated with higher odds of myopia, whereas office work, manual work, and unemployment were associated with lower odds than student status. Refractive errors were frequent among young adults attending tertiary ophthalmic clinics in Iraq. The observed associations with demographic, familial, social, and behavioral factors provide clinically useful information for targeted refractive assessment, counseling, and service planning in young adults. Population-based longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the generalizability and temporal nature of these associations.

papers.title: Latent profile analysis of sleep quality and its association with psychological resilience among emergency department nurses.
papers.abstract: Emergency department nurses are consistently exposed to high-intensity and high-pressure working conditions, leading to poor sleep quality. Psychological resilience can help alleviate the negative impacts of work stress. However, few studies have explored how resilience varies across distinct subgroups defined by different sleep profiles. This study employed latent profile analysis to identify distinct sleep-quality profiles among emergency department nurses and explored their association with psychological resilience to provide a basis for targeted interventions. From October to December 2025, 611 emergency nurses were recruited from 12 tertiary hospitals in Shandong through convenience sampling. Data were collected using a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Sleep quality profiles were determined through latent profile analysis, and associated factors were analyzed using multiple logistic regression. Emergency department nurses exhibited generally poor sleep quality, which was classified into four distinct profiles: "severely disturbed sleep" (8.0%), "sleep onset difficulty-sleep medication use" (15.1%), "mildly disturbed sleep" (26.7%), and "good sleep quality" (50.2%). Psychological resilience, age, work experience, monthly income, and monthly night shift number were significantly associated with these sleep quality profiles (p < 0.05). Emergency department nurses exhibit distinct sleep quality profiles. Targeted interventions addressing the specific factors associated with each subgroup could improve their sleep outcomes.

papers.title: Homeopathy for the treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a prevalent disorder associated with substantial impairment. Homeopathy has been proposed as a complementary treatment for insomnia, but its clinical effects remain uncertain. This systematic review assessed the efficacy, effectiveness, and safety of homeopathic treatments for insomnia. Prospective comparative studies evaluating any homeopathic preparation for insomnia were included. Searches in MEDLINE, EMBASE, seven additional databases, and three trial registries were conducted through August 2025. Risk of bias, intervention complexity, model validity, and pragmatism were assessed using respectively RoB 2, ROBINS-I, iCAT, MVHT, and RITES. Data were synthesized using random-effects meta-analyses, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs; n = 364 participants) and four non-randomized studies on interventions (NRSIs; n = 517) met the inclusion criteria. In adults, sleep quality (MD = -2.6 points; 95% CI -5.5 to 0.26; low certainty) and insomnia severity (MD = -3.2; 95% CI -5.68 to -0.72, moderate certainty) were reported in one RCT each. For total sleep time, the pooled MD of three RCTs was 0.65 hours (95% CI -0.9 to 2.2; low certainty). In children, one open-label RCT suggested a difference in insomnia severity, but certainty of evidence was very low. Adverse events were rarely reported, resulting in low certainty evidence. The current evidence is mainly limited by imprecision and risk of bias. The available evidence does not allow firm conclusions regarding the effects of homeopathy for insomnia. High-quality, replicated trials with systematic adverse-event monitoring are needed.

papers.title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in schizophrenia: enhancing transparency in clinical decision-making.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is a chronic and severe psychiatric disorder affecting nearly 1% of the global population, characterized by positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, negative symptoms including avolition and affective flattening, and cognitive impairments that compromise social and occupational functioning. Despite advances in psychiatry, diagnosis remains largely symptom-based, relying on criteria from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), highlighting the need for objective biomarkers and improved clinical decision support. Neuroimaging modalities, including structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI/fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), positron emission tomography (PET), as well as electrophysiological techniques such as electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG), have revealed abnormalities in brain connectivity, dopaminergic signaling, sensory processing, and network dysfunction associated with schizophrenia. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), have enabled prediction of diagnosis, treatment response, and relapse risk using multimodal clinical, neuroimaging, and genetic data. However, the "black-box" nature of many AI models limits transparency, interpretability, and clinician trust, restricting translation into practice. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses these challenges by providing interpretable, transparent, and clinically accountable models that support decision-making while preserving ethical and regulatory standards. By integrating explainable models with multimodal data, clinicians can use them as an adjunct for precision psychiatry, facilitating biomarker discovery, personalized treatment strategies, and trustworthy, actionable decisions, ultimately enhancing transparency and improving outcomes in schizophrenia care.

papers.title: Refined protocol for quantifying hippocampal neurogenesis in organotypic slice cultures.
papers.abstract: While human iPSC-derived models of the brain provide valuable genetic context, organotypic slice cultures from rodents remain essential for capturing the physiological complexity of intact neural tissue. This protocol describes a refinement of the interface method originally established by Stoppini and colleagues in 1991, providing a robust platform for the long-term cultivation of rodent hippocampal slices. Unlike dissociated monolayer systems, these 3-dimensional (3D) brain slices preserve the endogenous cytoarchitecture and the native extracellular matrix (ECM) of the central nervous system (CNS). This structural integrity is paramount for investigating hippocampal neurogenesis, as the proliferation, migration, and circuit integration of neural progenitors are governed by mechanical and biochemical cues present in the specialized local niche. By maintaining the spatial relationships between neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, this organotypic system replicates the arrangement of hippocampal neural networks more precisely than emergent stem cell models. Our protocol outlines an optimized workflow for McIlwain tissue chopper-based sectioning and maintenance of slices on porous hydrophilic membranes, ensuring efficient nutrient exchange and sustained tissue viability for several weeks. This configuration provides simultaneous access to the hippocampal slices and culture medium, facilitating the use of multiple investigative techniques such as live-cell imaging, electrophysiology, or pharmacological treatments. Despite relying predominantly on rodent tissue due to the scarcity of live human brain samples; the ability to observe developmental processes within the preserved architectural framework of the hippocampus makes this technique a cornerstone for studying neurogenesis and circuit assembly. Importantly, this refined approach bridges the gap between disorganised monolayers of in vitro neural networks and complex in vivo studies, offering accessible and reproducible physiological models to interrogate biochemical enhancers of neurogenesis or the pathological mechanisms of neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Adolescent non-suicidal self-injury scale - short form: revision and evaluation of its reliability and validity.
papers.abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a clinically significant concern among adolescents, and its accurate yet efficient assessment is essential for research, early identification, and intervention. Existing Chinese instruments-most notably the 19-item Adolescent Self-Harm Questionnaire (ASHS)-are relatively lengthy and ill-suited to rapid, large-scale screening. The present study had two aims: (a) to develop a short form of the ASHS, the Adolescent Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Scale-Short Form (ANSSI-SF), by integrating classical test theory (CTT) item analysis with genetic algorithm (GA) cross-validation, and (b) to evaluate its reliability, validity, and screening utility relative to the parent scale. Using a convenience sample of 1,090 primary and secondary school students, seven items-one for each of seven behavioral categories derived from a functional-typological framework of self-harm-were selected on the basis of CTT item statistics and GA cross-validation. The scale was evaluated through item analysis, internal-consistency and split-half reliability, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis (EFA/CFA), correlations with theoretically related constructs, known-groups comparisons (gender; smartphone addiction), and consistency and screening-accuracy analyses against the full 19-item ASHS. It indicated that all items demonstrated strong correlations with the total score, and both internal consistency and split-half reliability reached satisfactory levels.A unidimensional factor structure also exhibited good model fit. Additionally, scale scores were significantly positively correlated with related psychological indicators such as depression, anxiety, and sleep problems, and effectively differentiated differences in self-injurious behavior across gender and smartphone addiction groups.GA cross-validation confirmed that the selected items balanced parsimony with full coverage of all seven behavioral categories. These findings indicate that the ANSSI-SF is a brief, reliable, and valid instrument that preserves the content breadth of the parent ASHS while substantially reducing administration burden. It is well suited to rapid, large-scale screening and early identification of at-risk adolescents, facilitating timely referral and prevention. Limitations include convenience sampling from a single region and the absence of test-retest reliability; future research should validate the scale in clinical and diverse cultural samples and examine its predictive validity.

papers.title: Differential associations of the timing and amount of social media use with sleep quality and academic performance among undergraduate medical and dental students in Pakistan: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep and reduced academic performance among medical and dental students have been linked to social media use; however, whether the amount, purpose, and timing of use are independently associated with these outcomes remains unclear. In this cross-sectional study, 364 students enrolled in MBBS or BDS programs at ten institutions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, were recruited through convenience sampling and completed a paper-based questionnaire between October 2023 and April 2024. Sleep quality was measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and academic performance was assessed using self-reported percentage marks from the most recent professional examination. The models were adjusted for background characteristics and other social media exposures. Poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) was present in 312 students (85.7%, 95% CI 81.7-88.9). Duration of pre-sleep social media use was the only exposure independently associated with the PSQI global score (B = 1.594, 95% CI 1.081 to 2.106, p < 0.001), while total daily use was not. Conversely, each one-category increase in total daily use was associated with examination scores that were 1.40 percentage points lower (B = -1.404, 95% CI -2.053 to -0.756, p < 0.001). The classification of platform-derived purpose was not associated with either outcome; however, a secondary measure of purpose, the proportion of use devoted to academic work, was associated with a higher examination percentage (B = 2.148, 95% CI 1.513 to 2.782, p < 0.001). Thus, conclusions about purpose depended on how it was measured. Nocturnal checking was not associated with either outcome. Fitting both outcomes in a single model supported outcome specificity, most clearly for pre-sleep use (difference in standardized β = -0.271, p = 0.006; total daily use, 0.235, p = 0.023). Sleep quality was primarily associated with when social media was used, while examination performance was related to how much social media was used. These exploratory associations from a convenience sample cannot establish causal direction, apply to the participating institutions rather than to Pakistani students generally, and require replication with prospective designs and objective measures in future studies.

papers.title: Electrophysiological signature of stroke recovery: investigating EEG biomarkers for prognostic insights.
papers.abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, often resulting in persistent motor impairments that reflect disruptions in large-scale brain networks. An integrated framework capturing spatiotemporal EEG dynamics would help clarify how these networks change during recovery. We analysed resting-state EEG from stroke patients at 1 week (Session 1) and three months (Session 2) post-stroke to investigate electrophysiological biomarkers of motor recovery, indexed by change in the Fugl-Meyer scale (ΔFM). We quantified relative alpha-band power, microstate metrics (mean duration, complexity, and transition probabilities), and measures of metastability and synchrony derived from the Kuramoto Order Parameter. Change in relative alpha power emerged as the strongest single correlate of motor improvement, accounting for the largest proportion of variance among the EEG measures examined. Metastability and synchrony did not individually reach statistical significance but showed moderate positive correlations with ΔFM, particularly in the alpha and theta bands, and added 26% explained variance in ΔFM when combined with alpha power. Microstate parameters did not explain additional variance once alpha power and network-level dynamics were accounted for. A hierarchical model combining alpha power, metastability/synchrony, and microstates explained over 78% of the variance in ΔFM. These findings indicate that stroke recovery involves restoring balanced alpha oscillations and flexible large-scale brain coordination. Larger samples and more frequent longitudinal assessments are required to confirm the prognostic utility of integrated EEG biomarkers for guiding personalised stroke rehabilitation strategies.

papers.title: Irreversible functional network deformation induced by preprocessing scheme order in multivariate EEG recordings.
papers.abstract: The analysis of Electroencephalographic recordings is non-trivial, the order in which filtering and re-referencing are applied during multivariate signal preprocessing has a critical and underappreciated consequence for functional network estimation. Using EEG sleep recordings from healthy subjects, synthetic data from controlled numerical models (Nf-Tori and IAAFT surrogates), and surrogate-based statistical testing, we provide a quantitative comparison of two preprocessing schemes that differ solely in the order of filtering and re-referencing (filtering followed by re-referencing-FR, and re-referencing followed by filtering-RF). We show that the RF scheme induces spurious cross-correlations that increase systematically with the frequency band and are strongly modulated by the power spectral exponent β of the signal. Critically, for signals with steep power spectra (β ≥2), a regime that characterizes slow-wave sleep, epileptic post-ictal periods, anesthesia, neonatal, and patients in vegetative states, the RF scheme produces artificial correlations that are irreversible. They cannot be eliminated post-hoc even when surrogate-corrected cross-correlations (SAC-matrix) are applied. The mechanism underlying this effect is due to the high-amplitude slow-frequency components that dominate the median reference signal over extended time intervals, embedding redundant information across all channels. In contrast, the FR scheme introduces only small, systematic negative shifts in cross-correlations that are not statistically significant and can be effectively corrected using surrogate-based methods. We therefore recommend the FR scheme combined with surrogate-corrected cross-correlations for all applications involving signals with β ≥2. Although this finding is demonstrated in EEG, it applies to any multivariate recording where spatial re-referencing and band-pass filtering are applied sequentially.

papers.title: Virtual reality as a metacognitive training tool for lucid dreaming.
papers.abstract: Lucid dreaming (LD) involves awareness of being in a dream during REM sleep and depends on the reactivation of metacognitive and reality-monitoring processes. This study tested whether a virtual reality (VR) intervention designed to rehearse lucid-dream-relevant metacognitive routines increases LD rates beyond baseline training, and whether generic VR exposure produces similar effects. Thirty-eight participants with low previous LD experience completed a 5-week program of daily dream diaries and reality checks, assigned to: VR-experimental (n = 13), standard training plus eight LucidDreamingVR sessions preceded by brief open monitoring (OM) meditation; VR-control (n = 12), standard training plus eight LD-unrelated VR sessions; or Control (n = 13), standard training only. Dreams were classified as ordinary, semi-lucid, or lucid; semi-lucid and lucid dreams were treated as lucid-like. VR-experimental participants reported the highest number of lucid like dreams (26), followed by Control (11) and VR-control (4). A Poisson model with total recalled dreams as offset showed that lucid-like dream rates were significantly higher in VR-experimental than in VR-control, RR = 8.60, 95% CI [3.00, 24.64], p_Holm <0.001, and Control, RR = 4.00, 95% CI [1.97, 8.09], p_Holm <0.001. Responder rates showed a convergent pattern, with at least one lucid-like dream reported by 84.6% of VR-experimental participants, 61.5% of Control participants, and 33.3% of VR-control participants, showing that VR exposure alone was insufficient. Dream-oriented VR training preceded by OM meditation may facilitate LD by scaffolding metacognitive monitoring from wakefulness to REM sleep.

papers.title: Stress recovery and restorative effects of viewing different types of peony garden landscapes: a preliminary experiment.
papers.abstract: Substantial evidence supports the health benefits of urban green spaces, yet most studies focus on general landscapes, leaving a gap regarding specialized gardens with topographic variations (flatland, tableland, mountain land). This study explored the restorative effects of peony garden scenes with different topographic characteristics on students' physical and mental health using virtual reality (VR) and the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST). Participants (N = 56 per group, 23 ± 1.5 years old) were exposed to flatland peony garden (FPG), terraced peony garden (TPG), mountainous peony garden (MPG), or indoor environment (IE). Physiological factors were examined using heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), and electroencephalogram (EEG). psychological evaluation was carried out using the Profile of Mood States (POMS) and State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI). Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS) was used to assess subjective perceived recovery. Results showed that: (1) After TSST, HR, LF/HF, and Beta significantly increased (p < 0.01), while R-R, HF, and Alpha decreased (p < 0.01); (2) Compared to the stress stage, viewing FPG, TPG, and MPG led to significant physiological changes (p < 0.05), increased positive emotion (V-A, p < 0.01), and decreased negative emotions (A-H, F-I, T-A, C-B, D-D, anxiety, p < 0.01); (3) Perceived recovery was associated with emotional states, reflected in greater feelings of "being away" and "fascination." The most pronounced changes occurred in the MPG. In the current VR experiment, peony garden landscapes, especially those with abundant landscape elements and visual experience, exhibited therapeutic potential for short-term stress recovery compared with the windowless indoor office scene. The findings offer preliminary guidance for creating health-promoting peony garden landscapes.

papers.title: Effects of exercise on cognitive function in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the mediating role of sleep.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances affect nearly half of older adults and are linked to cognitive decline, yet the mechanistic pathways linking exercise to cognitive benefits remain poorly understood. We hypothesized that sleep quality mediates the exercise-cognition relationship in older adults. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, Embase, and PsycINFO from inception to June 2026 for randomized controlled trials examining structured exercise interventions (≥4 weeks) in adults aged ≥60 years that reported both cognitive and sleep outcomes. Random-effects meta-analyses and meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) were used to test the mediation hypothesis. Subgroup analyses examined baseline cognitive status and intervention duration. Eight studies (841 participants) were included. Exercise significantly improved cognitive function (SMD = 1.32, 95% CI: 0.70-1.94) and sleep quality (SMD = -1.13, 95% CI: -1.73 to -0.53). MASEM confirmed sleep quality as a significant partial mediator, with an indirect effect of β = 0.300 (95% CI: 0.125-0.404), accounting for 50.8% of the total cognitive benefit. The mediation proportion was larger in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (67.6%) than in cognitively healthy older adults (31.9%). Sleep quality significantly mediates the exercise-cognition relationship in older adults, accounting for approximately half of the cognitive benefit. These findings identify sleep as a candidate mechanistic target for optimizing exercise interventions, though larger mediation-designed trials are needed to confirm these exploratory estimates.

papers.title: Association of platelet-rich plasma combined with dorsal root ganglion-targeted pulsed radiofrequency with outcomes in subacute thoracic herpes zoster neuralgia: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Subacute herpes zoster neuralgia is a clinically important transitional stage before pain becomes fully established as persistent postherpetic neuralgia. In this single-center retrospective cohort study, patients with subacute thoracic herpes zoster neuralgia treated between January 2024 and December 2025 were identified from routine clinical records. Patients were classified according to the treatment received as PRP + PRF or PRF alone. The primary outcome was the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) score at 3 months after treatment. Repeated NRS and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) measurements were analyzed longitudinally. Secondary outcomes included pregabalin requirement and persistent clinically meaningful zoster-related pain, defined as NRS > 3 at the 3-month post-treatment follow-up. Seventy patients were analyzed, including 36 in the PRP + PRF group and 34 in the PRF group. At 3 months, the observed mean NRS score was lower in the PRP + PRF group than in the PRF group (1.39 ± 1.44 vs. 2.56 ± 1.02). In the prespecified ANCOVA adjusted for baseline NRS, PRP + PRF was associated with a lower 3-month NRS score than PRF alone (adjusted mean difference, -1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.71 to -0.54; p < 0.001). The association remained directionally consistent in additional multivariable and change-score sensitivity analyses. Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for NRS and PSQI, with lower NRS and PSQI scores in the PRP + PRF group from 1 week through 3 months. Pregabalin requirement at 3 months was lower in the PRP + PRF group (p = 0.001). Persistent clinically meaningful zoster-related pain at 3 months occurred in 4 of 36 patients (11.1%) in the PRP + PRF group and 7 of 34 patients (20.6%) in the PRF group (p = 0.336). In this retrospective cohort, PRP combined with DRG-targeted PRF was associated with faster early improvement in pain and sleep and with lower post-treatment pregabalin use than PRF alone. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and determine whether this approach influences progression to persistent pain and PHN.

papers.title: Constructing Built-in Hydroxyl Relay Through Ru/RuO2 Interfaces for Efficient PEM Water Electrolysis.
papers.abstract: As promising non-iridium alternatives, RuO2-based catalysts demonstrate superior acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity, however, their poor stability in acidic electrolyte remains a critical bottleneck hindering their application in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE). Herein, we construct a RuO2-based catalyst modified with Ru nanoparticles and grain boundaries (mG-RuO2) to simultaneously improve OER activity and stability. The resulting mG-RuO2 catalyst demonstrates superior acidic OER performance, requiring only 171 mV overpotential to reach 10 mA cm-2 and showing stable operation over 650 h. Theoretical calculations combined with in situ spectral analysis reveal that Ru nanoparticles not only break the H-bond network of water in the double-layer structure but also overcome the limitations of the adsorbate evolution mechanism pathway through efficient OH* spillover, thereby simultaneously enhancing the activity and stability of mG-RuO2. Moreover, the grain boundaries increase oxygen vacancies in RuO2, thereby suppressing the lattice oxygen mechanism and improving structural stability. More importantly, mG-RuO2 requires only 1.556 V to reach 1 A cm-2, while maintaining outstanding stability for over 500 h under this condition. This work elucidates the special OH* spillover mechanism in acidic OER, shedding light on the rational design of highly active, and stable RuO2-based electrocatalysts for PEMWE.

papers.title: Understanding MEG Source Profiles in Tuberous Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and medically refractory epilepsy are increasingly referred for epilepsy surgery, but presurgical evaluation is challenging due to multiple tubers and complex seizure onset zones. The aim of this retrospective study was to correlate key characteristics of magnetoencephalography (MEG) sources with intracranial EEG and surgical outcomes in patients with TSC. Patients with TSC and MRE who underwent MEG, stereo-EEG (sEEG) monitoring, and have at least 1-year postsurgical follow-up were included. MEG source number, laterality, location, and type (interictal or ictal) were compared with the seizure onset zones, defined by sEEG and postoperative seizure outcomes. Thirty-three patients (15 female patients and 18 male patients) (mean age 8.0 ± 8.2 years) were included. No significant correlation between the laterality of MEG sources (unilateral or bilateral) and surgical outcomes (χ2(1, n = 33) = 0.11, P = 0.75) was found, and there was no significant correlation between the number of MEG sources and surgical outcomes (P = 0.68). MEG-sEEG concordance scores showed a high specificity (86.7%) and positive predictive value (75%) as a predictor of postoperative seizure outcomes, and the concordance score was significantly higher in patients with an ictal MEG (4.4 (ictal) versus 3.0 [interictal]) (P = 0.04). This study demonstrates a localization concordance between MEG and sEEG that is related to postsurgical seizure outcomes in patients with TSC. However, no correlation between MEG source number, laterality (unilateral vs. bilateral), and surgical outcomes was found, supporting the continued use of MEG as a presurgical epilepsy tool in this patient population, no matter the number of potential source locations.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society

papers.title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Characteristics of Peripheral Neuropathy in Immune-Related Adverse Event of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: A Retrospective Study and Literature Review.
papers.abstract: To summarize clinical and laboratory characteristics of peripheral neurological immune-related adverse event (irAEs-PN) patients, to improve understanding and provide reference for early diagnosis of irAEs-PN caused by immune checkpoint inhibitors. We screened 61 patients with irAEs in our center from September 2020 to June 2025. In addition, studies with detailed clinical data related to irAEs-PN were collected in PubMed database from January 2015 to June 2025. A total of 50 patients with irAEs-PN were included, including 8 cases from our center and 42 cases reported in literature. The patients' demographic information, clinical characteristics, electrophysiological examination, therapy and outcomes were retrospectively analyzed and summarized. Among the eight patients in our center, the first symptom was paresthesia, occurring in two cases, and limb weakness, occurring in six cases. Electrophysiology identified two axonal neuropathies, three demyelinating, and three mixed axonal and demyelinating neuropathies. Among the 42 patients reported in literature, the first symptom was paresthesia, occurring in 39 cases, and limb weakness, occurring in 41 cases. Electromyography identified 13 axonal neuropathies, 25 demyelinating neuropathies, and 4 mixed axonal and demyelinating neuropathies. In most patients, irAEs-PN is characterized by demyelinating sensorimotor involvement of both the upper and lower limbs. In individuals receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, prompt electromyography after the onset of neuropathic symptoms can aid in detecting neurological involvement and facilitate earlier treatment.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society

papers.title: Sustained Seizure Freedom After Stereo-Electroencephalography Without Definitive Intervention: Evidence for Network Modulation by Invasive EEG.
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) is a diagnostic technique used to localize seizure-onset networks in drug-resistant epilepsy, typically guiding resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Sustained seizure freedom after diagnostic implantation alone is rarely described. We describe two patients who achieved long-term remission after sEEG monitoring without definitive surgical intervention. A 39-year-old man with posttraumatic right hemispheric epilepsy underwent implantation of 11 depth electrodes, during which no habitual seizures were captured despite medication withdrawal and provocation. After electrode explantation, he discontinued all antiseizure medications and has remained seizure-free for 71 months. A 63-year-old woman with left temporal epilepsy underwent implantation of 12 depth electrodes; monitoring again failed to capture habitual seizures, although abundant mesial temporal interictal discharges were recorded. After explantation, which was complicated by a small tract hemorrhage, she has remained seizure-free for 20 months on stable cenobamate therapy. These cases add to a limited body of evidence suggesting that sEEG implantation may induce microlesional or network-modulatory effects capable of interrupting seizure propagation, analogous to remission reported after intracranial electrode placement in prior series. Recognition of this phenomenon is clinically important. When no habitual seizures are recorded and early postoperative improvement is observed, a period of extended follow-up may be warranted before pursuing resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Further study is needed to define predictors of remission, clarify underlying mechanisms, and guide patient counseling regarding this uncommon but meaningful effect of invasive EEG.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society

papers.title: Effects of General Anaesthesia on the Sleep Structure of Patients With Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC) and are closely correlated with clinical outcomes. With an increasing number of pDoC patients undergoing surgery under general anaesthesia (GA), this study characterized sleep patterns in pDoC patients and evaluated the effects of GA on consciousness and nocturnal sleep. We prospectively enrolled 30 pDoC patients (14 in vegetative state [VS] and 16 in minimally conscious state [MCS]) undergoing spinal cord stimulation and 12 healthy controls. Among pDoC patients, 19 (10 VS, 9 MCS) with complete pre- and postoperative PSG data were analysed for GA effects. Controls underwent one overnight polysomnography (PSG); pDoC patients underwent pre- and postoperative PSG. Consciousness was assessed with Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) before and after surgery. Compared with controls, pDoC patients presented significantly impaired sleep structure, including reduced total sleep time (TST), decreased NREM Stage 2 sleep, diminished slow-wave sleep (SWS), reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration and percentage relative to TST (all p < 0.05). No significant short-term changes in CRS-R scores were observed following GA. Although GA significantly prolonged TST (p = 0.039), with numerical increases in absolute NREM and SWS durations, no statistically significant changes were observed in sleep stage percentages relative to TST (all p > 0.05). Subgroup analysis showed no significant within-group changes in sleep stage percentages in either the VS or MCS group. These findings suggest that GA increases TST without statistically significant changes in sleep structure in pDoC patients.

papers.title: Night work and differential effects on diurnal rhythms of cortisol, melatonin, and testosterone among permanent night-working men.
papers.abstract: Night work-induced circadian misalignment is associated with an increased risk of adverse health effects. It has been suggested that permanent night workers can entrain to being awake at night and therefore do not experience substantial circadian disruption in relation to night work. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of night work on diurnal rhythms of cortisol, melatonin, and testosterone among permanent night workers. Twenty-three men with permanent night work participated in this observational field study. They collected saliva every 4 hours over a 24-hour period for assessment of diurnal rhythms (mesor, amplitude and acrophase) on three days: the 2nd and 4th consecutive night shifts, and a day off. Within-person regression analyses with repeated measures adjusted for age were used to evaluate differences between the 2nd and 4th night shifts and between night shifts taken together versus days off. There were no statistically significant differences between diurnal rhythms on the 2nd and 4th consecutive night shifts. We observed differences in levels (mesor and amplitude) of cortisol and melatonin on night shifts compared to days off with the highest levels during work days. The timing (acrophase) of testosterone, but not cortisol and melatonin, differed between night shifts and days off. Thus, observed differences between the various hormonal diurnal rhythms to night work indicate internal desynchronization. Studies of how diurnal rhythms of multiple biological systems are affected by night work and the link to health effects are warranted to further elucidate the mechanisms linking night work to adverse health effects.
papers.journal: Scandinavian journal of work, environment & health

papers.title: Migration Characteristics and Mechanism of Active Components From Jieyu Anshen Granule in Different Insomnia Mouse Models.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent disorder with substantial health and socioeconomic impacts, for which traditional Chinese medicine is an important treatment option. Jieyu Anshen Granule (JYAS-G) shows excellent clinical efficacy in insomnia treatment, but its active components, in vivo migration characteristics and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Two mouse insomnia models induced by p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA, chemical method) and sleep deprivation machine (SDM, physical method) were established respectively, and mice were administered with low and high doses of JYAS-G, with open field test used to evaluate the pharmacodynamic effects. UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS combined with GNPS was applied to systematically identify the in vitro components of JYAS-G and its migration profiles in mouse plasma, liver, heart, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and hypothalamus. The SDM model induced insomnia with manic-like behaviors, which were significantly ameliorated by JYAS-G, whereas the PCPA model produced no significant insomnia-like phenotypes under the current conditions. In total, 89 in vitro components and 43 blood-absorbed components of JYAS-G were identified, showing marked tissue-specific distribution. Network pharmacology and molecular docking identified core components, including furanogermenone and curcumenol, predicted to exert anti-insomnia effects by targeting ADORA2A, GABRB3, and SLC6A4 and regulating the neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathway. This study characterizes the in vivo migration characteristics of JYAS-G and provides insights into its multi-target anti-insomnia mechanism, while comparing the modeling differences between two common insomnia animal models. These findings provide scientific evidence for the rational clinical application and further development of JYAS-G.
papers.journal: Rapid communications in mass spectrometry : RCM

papers.title: An Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer for Participant-Level Classification of Depressive Symptoms From Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive modality for investigating depressive symptoms; however, conventional deep-learning methods often require large labeled datasets and provide limited interpretability. We developed an Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer Network for participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG. The framework employed masked temporal modeling for self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Model performance was evaluated using repeated nested participant-wise cross-validation and compared with conventional machine-learning and deep-learning baselines. Explainability was investigated through transformer attention maps and SHAP-based channel attribution. The proposed model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73-0.90), a precision-recall AUC of 0.69, balanced accuracy of 0.75, sensitivity of 0.72, and specificity of 0.78. The positive predictive value was 0.57, indicating a substantial false-positive burden in the evaluated cohort. The proposed model showed the highest point-estimate ROC-AUC among the evaluated baselines, with a 0.07 improvement over EEGNet; however, the overlapping uncertainty intervals and the small elevated-symptom cohort warrant cautious interpretation of comparative superiority. Performance decreased from an ROC-AUC of 0.82 in Run 1 to 0.78 in Run 2 and to 0.72-0.73 under cross-condition transfer, supporting interpretation of these analyses as internal reproducibility and condition-shift assessments rather than independent external validation. Removing self-supervised pretraining reduced the ROC-AUC to 0.74. Explainability analyses identified distributed temporally relevant intervals and frontal-midline to centro-parietal channel contributions, with attribution interpreted as model-relevance evidence rather than causal biomarker evidence. Overall, the findings provide preliminary internal evidence that self-supervised temporal representation learning can support participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG under the evaluated experimental conditions. The findings do not establish clinical diagnostic validity, screening readiness, or independent external generalizability.
papers.journal: International journal of methods in psychiatric research

papers.title: Overview of the Mechanistic Potential of Serotonin Reuptake Transporters in Depression.
papers.abstract: Depression is considered to be one of the most common psychiatric disorders that affect millions of people, despite a large amount of unrecorded data. This disorder has been associated with feelings of hopelessness, sleep disturbances, and even suicidal thoughts. However, the serotonin hypothesis emerged in the 1960s, suggesting that serotonin was one of the key neurotransmitters associated with depression by regulating mood, emotion, and cognitive effects. The serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT) plays a vital role in maintaining homeostasis by facilitating the reuptake of synaptic serotonin into presynaptic neurons. The dysregulation of SERT has been potentially involved in the pathophysiology of depressive disorder and its related disorders. This manuscript provides an overview of the pharmacological aspects of SERT, including its mechanism of action, regulation, role in depression, and potential therapeutic targets. Current antidepressant research is increasingly focused on the development of highly selective and rapid-acting modulators of the SERT to overcome the delayed onset of action and limited efficacy associated with conventional selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Emerging strategies include designing allosteric SERT inhibitors that bind to alternative sites on the transporter, potentially enhancing selectivity while minimizing adverse effects. In parallel, the integration of pharmacogenomic insights into clinical practice seeks to personalize antidepressant therapy based on individual genetic variations-particularly polymorphisms in the SLC6A4 gene and related molecular markers-thereby improving therapeutic precision and overall treatment outcomes. Allosteric modulation of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and pharmacogenomics- guided treatment selection highlight the need to maximize therapeutic outcomes and fulfill the unmet needs of patients who suffer from depression.

papers.title: Non-linear Age-related Patterns of Sleep Architecture in First-episode Schizophrenia: A Restricted Cubic Spline Analysis.
papers.abstract: The dynamic relationship between age and sleep architecture in the early stages of schizophrenia remains poorly characterized. Traditional linear models may fail to capture the complex patterns of sleep stages across different age groups. This study aimed to examine the non-linear associations between age and sleep parameters in First-Episode Schizophrenia (FES) patients. A total of 109 FES patients were recruited, and the objective sleep parameters were measured using Polysomnography (PSG). The Restricted Cubic Spline (RCS) analysis was employed to investigate the non-linear patterns of sleep stages across the observed age range (14-45 years), controlling for biological sex, Body Mass Index (BMI), and duration of illness. RCS analysis suggested statistically significant non-linear associations between age and selected sleep parameters. Specifically, the relationship between age and percentage of N3 sleep (N3P) demonstrated a U-shaped pattern (pnon-linearity =0.0007), with an estimated nadir at approximately 31.1 years, after which N3P appeared to stabilize or modestly increase. The slope was negative below approximately 31.1 years and positive above this age point. For the percentage of N2 sleep (N2P), the spline curve showed an inverted U-shaped cross-sectional association between age and N2P (pnon-linearity =0.03). N2P was highest among individuals in their early 30s, peaking at an inflection point of 31.3 years and relatively lower among both younger and older FES patients. No significant non-linear relationships were observed for Arousal Time (AT) and percentage of REM (REMP) (all p > 0.05). In FES patients, the relationship between age and sleep architecture was characterized by distinct non-linear age-related patterns rather than simple linear associations. The age of approximately 31 years appeared to be a critical inflection point for both N2 and N3 sleep stages in FES patients. These findings provide a more nuanced description of the sleep profile in early-stage SZ.

papers.title: Sleep Is Integral to School Health and Adolescent Wellbeing: An Evidence-Based Call to Action.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for healthy growth and function. Sleepiness is common in middle and high school classrooms; many adolescents struggle to receive sufficient, well-timed sleep. We provide a discussion of theory and policy ramifications of adolescent sleep science. We provide a unified overview of sleep's benefits for physical and mental health, safety, alertness, learning, and school performance. We outline the developmental biological-social-societal interplay influencing sleep in adolescents. We discuss the impact of changing school start times on sleep health and factors relating to school-related sleep equity. We discuss the success of changing school start times, sleep-health education, and how science-informed policies can combine later start times with educational and behavioral supports. Ignoring sleep compromises students' and schools' success. Improving the opportunity for sleep, primarily through altering school start times, yields healthier and more productive students. Whether action manifests in the classroom, school, district, or state, the health of students-and schools-improves when policies offer adolescents opportunities to obtain the sleep they need. Underscoring sleep's critical role in school performance, the evidence calls on educators and policymakers to address chronic sleep deprivation and its consequences for adolescents.

papers.title: Mismatch Responses to Prosodic Changes in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: A Longitudinal Approach.
papers.abstract: Developmental language disorder is characterized by difficulties in auditory processing and prosody discrimination. Estonian word prosody features a unique three-way quantity distinction, characterized by changes in syllable duration and pitch contour, which differentiate word meaning and grammatical cases. In this study, we examined the Mismatch Responses longitudinally in 23 children with developmental language disorder and 25 age and biological sex matched typically developing peers (age at first measurement 4;6-6;5 years; age at second measurement 5;6-7;5 years). A multifeature paradigm was used in which all stimuli were meaningful words; two deviants differed from the standard, one in syllable duration and the other in both syllable duration and pitch contour. We also tested the discrimination of these prosodic features with behavioral tasks at both measurements. For duration discrimination, an early positive mismatch response diminished from first to second measurement, while a subsequent negative mismatch response increased. Significant longitudinal changes were observed in the typically developing group but not in children with developmental language disorder, while direct comparisons of maturational trajectories did not reveal significant group differences. For the duration and pitch contrast, in both groups and at both assessments, no mismatch response was detected. Additionally, no association was observed at the individual level between maturational changes in mismatch responses and behavioral discrimination at either measurement. These findings provide insights into the maturation of prosodic change detection processes and contribute to a better understanding of developmental language disorder and its manifestations.

papers.title: The Effects of Positive Airway Pressure on the Middle Ear: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: To systematically review the literature evaluating the effects of positive airway pressure (PAP) on the middle ear and to perform a meta-analysis of its impact on middle ear pressure (MEP), tympanic membrane (TM) morphology, and hearing outcomes. Pubmed, MEDLINE, OVID, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. A systematic search was performed from database inception through November 1, 2025, following PRISMA guidelines. Studies reporting quantitative middle ear outcomes following PAP were included. Meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model of MEP, TM retraction grade, and pure tone average (PTA). Nine studies met inclusion criteria. PAP therapy demonstrated a significant dose-dependent increase in MEP (R2 = 0.9516, p < 0.0001). Meta-analysis of MEP at a setting of 10 cm H20 showed a pooled mean increase of 51.4 daPa (p < 0.00001). Swallowing was found to be a prerequisite for significant pressure transfer to the middle ear. In patients with Eustachian tube dysfunction and TM retraction, continuous PAP use was associated with significant morphological improvement in TM retractions (p = 0.002) and a mean improvement in PTA of 7.3 dB HL (95% CI 3.45, 11.17, p = 0.0002). PAP increases MEP in a dose-dependent manner, a finding of interest to otologic surgeons. In addition to its role in sleep medicine, PAP therapy may serve as a noninvasive treatment for chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction and TM retraction. Further prospective studies are needed to guide management conclusions for otologic patients utilizing PAP, particularly in the postoperative setting.

papers.title: The Neural Symphony in the Periodontium: Health, Inflammation, and Regeneration.
papers.abstract: Periodontal nerves, comprising sensory, sympathetic, and parasympathetic fibers, are essential components of the periodontium. Beyond their classic sensory and proprioceptive functions, these neural networks actively modulate periodontal immune responses, bone remodeling, and tissue regeneration. They orchestrate tissue homeostasis by releasing specific neuropeptides, neurotransmitters, and neurotrophic factors. The progression of periodontitis is intimately linked to neural dysregulation, where proinflammatory mediators (e.g., excessive substance P and sympathetic catecholamines) overpower protective signals (e.g., calcitonin gene-related peptide and parasympathetic acetylcholine). Conversely, successful periodontal regeneration requires the restoration of this neural equilibrium. Nerve terminals rapidly sprout into osteogenic zones during early repair. Subsequently, their spatiotemporally patterned signaling suppresses osteoclastogenesis and promotes the osteogenic differentiation of stem cells.
