Crucially, these local neural networks function as a bidirectional conduit linking the periodontium to the central nervous system: systemic stressors (eg, sleep deprivation and chronic stress) can compromise ganglionic autophagy or trigeminal function to exacerbate periodontal bone loss, while periodontal pathogens can reciprocally exploit these pathways to induce central neuroinflammation. Recognizing this interconnected oral-neural-brain axis not only explains why certain periodontitis-susceptible patients remain refractory to conventional therapies but also highlights the broader impact of periodontal inflammation on neurodegenerative risk. Furthermore, nerve-targeted strategies, including neurotrophin-functionalized biomaterials, local neuropeptide delivery, and bioelectric neuromodulation, offer promising approaches to resolving refractory inflammation, restoring periodontal integrity, and concurrently mitigating the risk of associated central neuroinflammation. In this review, we comprehensively characterize the spatiotemporal plasticity of periodontal nerves under physiological and pathological conditions. We dissect the molecular mechanisms linking neural signaling to periodontal immunity and repair, and highlight how integrating neurobiology into periodontology could advance the development of next-generation regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Composite sleep score and risk of psychiatric disorders via proteomic features in preclinical obesity: a prospective cohort study from the UK Biobank.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are linked to psychiatric disorders, and obesity is associated with a higher risk of several psychiatric disorders. However, evidence is lacking on how a composite sleep score relates to psychiatric disorder risk in preclinical obesity and on the proteomic pathways that mediate this relationship. Our study aimed to investigate the association of composite sleep score and the risk of multiple specific psychiatric disorders in participants with preclinical obesity. The prospective cohort study from the UK Biobank included 91,380 participants with preclinical obesity. Six groups were categorized according to sleep scores. Hazard ratios (HRs) for the incidence risk of psychiatric disorders were estimated using multiple Cox proportional hazards regression analysis. Mediation analysis of plasma proteomics in this association was conducted in a subset of participants (n = 9,486). After a mean follow-up period of 12.9 years, a total of 8,992 incident cases of psychiatric disorders were observed. Using Group 1 as the reference, the risk of psychiatric disorders decreased significantly across Groups 2-6 with increasing sleep score, reaching the lowest in Group 6 (fully adjusted HR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.33-0.67). Analyses of specific psychiatric disorders revealed that the inverse associations remained significant after full adjustment, with the most notable effect observed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (HR = 0.24, 95% CI: 0.08-0.72). Mediation analysis further identified 16 plasma proteins that exerted significant partial mediating effects in this association. Our findings underscore that better sleep quality is associated with a lower risk of psychiatric disorders among individuals with preclinical obesity. The identification of proteomic mediators may provide further insight into the underlying biological mechanisms, highlighting the clinical significance of integrating sleep-related assessment and intervention.

papers.title: An EEG-based framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis via single-channel multi-entropy fusion and ensemble learning.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, and its early diagnosis is vital for timely intervention. However, most existing EEG-based diagnostic methods rely on multi-channel devices confined to hospital settings, limiting their accessibility for community screening. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a lightweight processing approach for portable, low-cost devices to support early AD diagnosis using single-channel EEG data, integrating signal purification with complementary entropy-based feature extraction and ensemble learning. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into five brain rhythms (δ, θ, α, β, γ) using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is then applied to extract Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) from the selected rhythm. Four entropy measures, including Differential Entropy (DE), Singular Spectral Entropy (SSE), Fuzzy Entropy (FE), and Sample Entropy (SE), are subsequently extracted from each IMF to construct the Multi-IMF Entropy Matrix (MIMFEM). After that, an ensemble learning framework combining five classifiers is designed to discriminate AD patients from healthy controls (HCs). The proposed method is evaluated on two public datasets using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). Using single-channel EEG data, our approach achieves classification accuracies of 97.92% on the Florida-based dataset and 81.54% on the AHEPA dataset, with corresponding F1-scores of 97.87% and 82.86%, respectively. These results, achieved with limited data sources, show that our approach provides an effective, practical solution for single-channel wearable AD screening and addresses the critical need for low-cost, accessible early diagnostic tools, advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare through a lightweight model.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers. Part H, Journal of engineering in medicine

papers.title: Acute Onset Orolingual Choreoathetosis and Auditory Hallucinations in a Healthy Young Adult Following High Melatonin Dose.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is considered a safe OTC sleep aid with rarely reported adverse effects despite limited data. We present a case of acute orolingual choreoathetosis and auditory hallucinations following 132 mg ingestion of melatonin in an otherwise healthy, 22-year-old active-duty male in IBOLC training. The patient developed abrupt, predominantly orolingual choreoathetosis and mild auditory hallucinations, 1 hour after waking. Three days earlier, he began taking 24 mg of melatonin nightly for insomnia and ingested 132 mg the night before presentation. He denied alcohol, illicit drug, or other medication use. On ED arrival, he was hemodynamically stable with continuous orolingual choreoathetosis. Initial labs demonstrated mild acute kidney injury and transaminitis. Head CT was unremarkable. MRI head showed a nonspecific left frontal white matter hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed normal protein and WBC, negative culture, and negative oligoclonal bands, though CSF processing difficulties prevented autoimmune panel completion. Neurologic symptoms resolved by the next morning without recurrence, and a subsequent EEG was unremarkable. This case documents a temporal association between high-dose melatonin exposure and acute neurologic symptoms but does not establish melatonin as the cause. The clinical presentation also occurred in the setting of substantial confounders, including sleep deprivation and heat exposure. This observation supports further investigation of uncommon neurologic presentations occurring after high-dose melatonin intake.

papers.title: Surgical management of periorbital non-traumatic subcutaneous emphysema during continuous positive airway pressure.
papers.abstract: A 47-year-old male requested treatment for recurrent, rapid left upper eyelid swelling due to subcutaneous emphysema (SE) with use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for treatment of obstructive sleep apnoea. There was no previous history of facial trauma or surgery. Computerised tomography revealed pneumatisation of the lacrimal sac fossa and nasolacrimal duct with a prominent agger nasi air cell medial to the lacrimal sac extending down the nasolacrimal duct. He underwent endoscopic surgery to reduce the pneumatisation superomedial to the lacrimal sac. The subcutaneous emphysema significantly improved, only now occurring with very high CPAP pressure. Periorbital and orbital emphysema are typically secondary to trauma or iatrogenic causes. To the best of our knowledge, only one case of periorbital, non-traumatic emphysema secondary to CPAP has been reported. This is the first case to describe surgical reduction of a pneumatised lacrimal sac fossa to successfully treat CPAP-related non-traumatic subcutaneous emphysema.

papers.title: Staff Perspectives of Implementing a Community-Based Stroke Recovery Program in Regional Australia: A Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: To describe the experience of non-government organisation (NGO) staff implementing a community-based stroke recovery program based on the principles of environmental enrichment. A qualitative descriptive study to capture staff experiences. Semi-structured interviews with staff were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. A community-based NGO service in regional New South Wales, Australia. Eight staff members employed in a regional NGO and involved in the implementation of the program, including a program coordinator, a physiotherapist, allied health assistants, creative artists and managers. Four themes were identified: (1) We've got a great space here-highlighted the importance of the physical environment, access and location; (2) There's an order to it-described the program's strong foundations formed through training, defined processes and support; (3) We make it work-demonstrated the flexibility and adaptability of staff in responding to individual needs and overcoming challenges and (4) Enriching lives-captured the sense of community, positivity and recovery outcomes. Staff experiences aligned closely with self-determination theory, reflecting feelings of capability, confidence and connection. Staff in a regional NGO felt well-supported and capable of delivering a community-based stroke program. This demonstrates the potential role NGO services may play in addressing gaps in stroke recovery care in regional Australia. The methods used in this study can be used to implement this and other similar community-based programs with NGO services in the future.
papers.journal: The Australian journal of rural health

papers.title: Impact of environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing on the transcriptome of three porcine brain tissues.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment and mixing represent two management procedures in pig production with opposing effects: while environmental enrichment can promote welfare by reducing stress, repeated mixing often induces stress and can negatively impact welfare. Despite their importance in pig husbandry, how these opposing management procedures affect brain function at the molecular level remains poorly understood. This study investigated how environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing influence gene expression patterns across three porcine brain regions: hypothalamus, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Using RNA sequencing, we analyzed brain tissues from 48 gilts subjected to a 2 × 2 factorial design comparing enrichment conditions (enriched vs. barren) and allostatic load (repeated vs. minimal mixing). While environmental enrichment showed minimal impact on gene expression, allostatic load resulted in 38 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus, primarily involved in hormone regulation, protein transport, and neuronal activity. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules moderately correlated with experimental conditions: six modules in hippocampus associated with allostatic load, and four modules in hypothalamus associated with enrichment. Functional annotation revealed that these modules were primarily enriched in biological processes related to synaptic signaling, neuron development, and metabolic activity. Hub genes from these modules were identified, and turned out not to overlap with differentially expressed genes. Our findings suggest that based on this experimental design, the hippocampus may be particularly responsive to stress-induced transcriptomic changes, while the molecular effects of the environmental enrichment appear more subtle. Overall, this study reveals limited but region-specific transcriptional responses to allostatic load in the porcine brain.

papers.title: Exploring the feasibility, safety and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted temporal interference stimulation for major depressive disorder: a pilot study.
papers.abstract: Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a novel noninvasive neuromodulation technique. However, whether it can be applied in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. This pilot study investigated the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical effects of amygdala-targeted TIS in patients with MDD. In this single-center, single-arm pilot study, 32 MDD patients received a 5-day amygdala-targeted TIS. The primary outcomes were feasibility (defined by the intervention completion rate) and safety (evaluated through participant-reported adverse events). The secondary outcomes assessed preliminary clinical efficacy, including changes in depressive symptoms measured by the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17) and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), as well as anxiety, anhedonia, sleep quality, and health-related quality of life. Assessments were performed at baseline, postintervention, and at the 1-week and 1-month follow-ups. Statistical analyses included mainly linear mixed-effects models and paired t tests. All participants completed the full intervention while maintaining stable psychiatric medication. TIS was well tolerated, with mostly mild adverse events (sleepiness, 24.1%; dizziness, 14.1%; unusual scalp sensations, 10.5%) and no serious safety concerns. The HAMD-17 response rates were 59.4% post-intervention, 65.4% at the 1-week follow-up, and 50.0% at the 1-month follow-up. The corresponding MADRS response rates were 54.8%, 65.4%, and 53.3%, respectively. Significant improvements were also observed in anxiety, anhedonia, sleep quality, and quality of life. This pilot study suggests that amygdala-targeted TIS is feasible, well tolerated, and associated with promising clinical improvements in patients with MDD, warranting further investigation in randomized controlled trials. This study has been prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on June 14, 2024 (Registration ID: NCT06461260).
